title: Aequorin and green fluorescent protein from Friday Harbor jellyfish
people: Osamu Shimomura, Frank H. Johnson, Yo Saiga, Akemi Shimomura, William W. (Bill) Ward, John R. Blinks, S. Inouye, Douglas C. Prasher, Milton J. Cormier, Martin Chalfie, Roger Y. Tsien, E. Newton Harvey
summary: Jellyfish from Friday Harbor yielded aequorin, a protein that gives off light when it meets calcium, and green fluorescent protein (GFP), later used to track gene activity and proteins in living cells. A 1921 paper by E. Newton Harvey, from the marine station at Friday Harbor, recorded bluish-green light in the jellyfish *Aequorea*, with no stated link to the later work. In summer 1961 Osamu Shimomura, working at FHL with Frank Johnson, found that calcium triggered the light, and their group made an extract from about 10,000 jellyfish. Purification at Princeton yielded aequorin, with GFP as a byproduct, and was reported in 1962. Later harvests supplied chemical studies. By Shimomura's own dating, a molecule called coelenterazine was identified in 1975 as the light-emitting part of aequorin, and a 1978 paper named the peroxide form of that molecule as the active group. Only one source, the FHL centennial timeline by Mills and Hermans, records Bill Ward processing about 70,000 jellyfish a year for GFP work, nearly every summer from 1975 to 1993. In 1985 the groups of S. Inouye and Douglas Prasher separately cloned the gene for aequorin, and in 1992 Prasher's group cloned the gene for GFP, all from Friday Harbor animals.
significance: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences' Scientific Background to the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to Shimomura, Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien, credits tools based on GFP with tracking gene activity and proteins in living cells. It says that without Shimomura's work the field would likely have been delayed by decades. It also credits Davenport and Nicol (1955) with first describing the green light of *Aequorea*, although Harvey had recorded bluish-green light in 1921. Where Davenport and Nicol's animals came from, and so whether their paper has any FHL tie, is not established. Shimomura's Nobel lecture records that aequorin was the first photoprotein (a self-contained light-emitting protein) to be discovered, and that it became an important probe for detecting calcium after work by Ridgway and Ashley in 1967.
fhl_tie: Shimomura found the calcium trigger at FHL in 1961. His group collected about 850,000 jellyfish there through 1988 and did the first processing there, over 19 trips by his count; other sources give 18 or about 20 summers. FHL thus supplied the animals, a laboratory site and the first steps of the work. Purification and chemistry were done mainly at Princeton, then Woods Hole, and the genes were cloned in the US state of Georgia, in Japan and at Woods Hole. Chalfie and Tsien used Prasher's clone of the GFP gene at Columbia and San Diego. The FHL centennial timeline and a 2008 newsletter, both from Claudia Mills, say the two also worked at FHL. Their Nobel lectures and biographies do not mention such work, and the claim is unconfirmed. A 2018 FHL news item, Tide Bite, places GFP's isolation at FHL in 1962, which conflicts with Shimomura's own accounts of extraction in 1961 and purification at Princeton.

title: Giant barnacle muscle and the calcium signal in contraction
people: Graham Hoyle, Thomas Smyth Jr., Joe Connell, Ellis B. Ridgway, Christopher C. Ashley, Joel E. Brown, John R. Blinks, Reinhardt Rüdel, Stuart R. Taylor, John E. Desmedt, Karl Hainaut, D. Lansing Taylor, George Reynolds
summary: The calcium signal inside single muscle cells was recorded by injecting a barnacle's giant fibers with aequorin, a jellyfish protein that gives off light with calcium. Graham Hoyle and Thomas Smyth described the fibers in *Balanus nubilus* in 1963. Ellis Ridgway and Christopher Ashley reported brief calcium signals in 1967, and their 1970 paper, recording calcium and tension together, suggested that calcium controls the rate of force development. Calcium's role was already suspected, and Jöbsis and O'Connor reported its release in toad muscle in 1966. Joel Brown and John Blinks took aequorin to light-sensing cells (1974), and Blinks and colleagues to frog and toad fibers (1978). Desmedt and Hainaut (1977) concluded from barnacle fibers that the muscle relaxant dantrolene rather selectively inhibits calcium release. In the amoeba *Chaos carolinensis*, D. Lansing Taylor, Blinks and Reynolds (1980) reported a calcium signal during movement, while Cobbold (1980) saw no signal change.
significance: Osamu Shimomura, who isolated aequorin, called the 1967 note the first report of aequorin used to study intracellular calcium and wrote in 1995 that hundreds of papers followed. His 2008 Nobel lecture cites it as the point when the protein's value as a calcium probe became clear. A 1990 review by Blinks, himself a participant, records photoproteins (light-emitting proteins such as aequorin) used as calcium indicators in almost every kind of cell, most widely in muscle. Szentesi and colleagues (2001) list the 1977 dantrolene paper among results in barnacle and frog fibers not confirmed in mammalian preparations, and call the drug's site of action controversial.
fhl_tie: FHL supplied barnacles. Station accounts trace Hoyle's interest in these barnacles to a gathering hosted by Joe Connell at FHL, dated 1960, the early 1960s or 1963, though Hoyle and Smyth had already described the fibers in a January 1963 Science note, from Oregon and Penn State, which rules out summer 1963. Their paper of December 1963 carries an FHL address. FHL's own program review says aequorin was first used in barnacle fibers at Friday Harbor, but Ridgway and Ashley's 1967 and 1968 notes carry addresses at the University of Oregon in Eugene, and FHL barnacles also went there, so that site rests on the station's account alone. Later papers from Mayo, Brussels and Harvard used aequorin from Friday Harbor jellyfish and some thank FHL, but no source places those experiments there.

title: How commensal worms find their hosts
people: Demorest Davenport, John F. Hickok, Ronald V. Dimock Jr.
summary: Experiments at Friday Harbor indicated that some commensal scale worms, which live on a host animal without harming it, pick out that host by a chemical cue in the water. Demorest Davenport started in summer 1949, asking how these worms stay with one host when related species sit beside it. Building on Welsh's work with freshwater mites, he designed a glass Y-tube that made single worms choose between two streams of water. *Arctonoe fragilis* from the sea star *Evasterias* entered the host arm in 33 of 35 runs, and cross tests indicated that this host's attractant differs from that of the sea cucumber *Stichopus*. With John Hickok in summer 1950 he found the cue unstable and lost when hosts were disturbed, while another worm, *Halosydna*, showed no response at a distance. In 1956 the pair compared populations within species, some only in brief preliminary tests. Ronald Dimock and Davenport reported in 1971 that *A. pulchra* kept for weeks on another host could lose or switch its preference.
significance: Caulier and colleagues (2013), who identified saponins as the host cue for a symbiotic crab, tested in what they call the Davenport olfactometer and cite the 1950, 1951 and 1971 papers. Uchida (1983) names *Arctonoe* as the most closely examined host-guest case in bristle worms and credits these papers for its sensing of host chemicals. Recognition rests on this use and citation: 65 in OpenAlex for the 1950 paper, 9 by Davenport or his coauthors. Davenport (1950) knew of no earlier experiments on marine partnerships. Orton and Smith (1935) had run brief tests, but he later said no data were presented.
fhl_tie: The 1950 paper says its studies were done at the University of Washington's Oceanographic Laboratories at Friday Harbor, and the 1957 paper dates the start to summer 1949. The 1951 and 1957 papers place experiments there in summers 1950 and 1956. In a 1966 chapter Davenport, whose address was the University of California, Santa Barbara, wrote that the series had been done mostly at FHL. Two later papers of the series (1953) were done at the Plymouth Laboratory, and the 1957 paper says the studies continued at Santa Barbara. The 1971 work ran at Friday Harbor and Santa Barbara. Its host-switching tests used Santa Barbara hosts and appear to have run there, though the paper does not say so.

title: Nerve-free conduction and dual spikes in jellyfish
people: George O. Mackie, L. M. Passano, Robert W. Meech, P. A. H. Kerfoot, Alan Roberts, C. L. Singla, R. M. Marx
summary: Some jellyfish and their relatives conduct electrical impulses through sheets of cells without nerves, and in one jellyfish a single nerve fiber can carry two kinds of impulse. In 1968, George Mackie and L. M. Passano showed that in small jellyfish such as *Sarsia*, nerve-free epithelia (sheets of covering cells) conduct impulses that do not fade and have no fixed direction. In 1973, Mackie recorded action potentials, the impulses of nerve cells, from a giant fiber in the siphonophore *Nanomia*, a colonial relative of jellyfish. In the jellyfish *Aglantha digitale*, P. A. H. Kerfoot had noticed an odd second signal. In 1985, Mackie and Robert Meech reported that one giant motor axon (a nerve fiber driving muscle) carries a fast sodium action potential for escape swimming and a small calcium spike, another brief impulse, for slow swimming. They called this the first report of an axon with two kinds of impulse. In a series of papers from 1995 to 2003 titled Central Circuitry, Mackie, Meech and colleagues traced the pathways in *Aglantha* for locomotion, feeding and tentacle contraction, and Mackie's 2004 review counts twelve conduction systems of nerve cells and two of epithelia.
significance: The Royal Society's citation for Mackie, elected a Fellow in 1991, credits him as the first to show that epithelial cells propagate action potentials and names the separate sodium and calcium spikes in one axon among his discoveries. His memoir, though, notes earlier speculation about nerve-like conduction going back to G. H. Parker and independent work by Alan Roberts on tadpole skin. Alcami and El Hady's 2019 review of how axons process signals uses *Aglantha* as its example of sodium and calcium spikes traveling in one axon.
fhl_tie: Mackie, visiting from the University of Alberta and then Victoria, began work on *Nanomia* at FHL in 1961 and teamed up there with Passano on jellyfish. The 1968, 1973 and 1985 papers used animals from the FHL dock, and the 1985 Nature letter thanks FHL for hospitality during the work. Mackie's memoir places the 1984 *Aglantha* experiments and later circuitry work at FHL, and Meech wrote in 2022 that much of the *Aglantha* work was done there. Both authors took part in that work, so these are insiders' accounts. The first electrical proof of epithelial conduction came from siphonophore recordings at Villefranche in 1963–64, so the Royal Society's "first" is not an FHL result. A timeline co-written by Mills, Mackie's student, says the work behind Mackie's Fellowship, on tunicates and jellyfish, was largely at FHL, but the memoir places siphonophore work and work on the tunicate *Pyrosoma* at Villefranche and says *Corella*, another tunicate, was collected at Victoria.

title: Identified neurons and behavior in the sea slug *Tritonia*
people: A. O. Dennis Willows, Graham Hoyle, Derek A. Dorsett, Peter A. Getting
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Dennis Willows found large, identifiable nerve cells in the brain of the sea slug *Tritonia* and showed that stimulating a single one could trigger a movement such as turning or swimming. As a University of Oregon graduate student of Graham Hoyle, working at FHL about 1964, he dissected, at Hoyle's suggestion, a large slug trawled from East Sound and saw large cell bodies on its brain. Recordings with microelectrodes in further animals showed that these cells were neurons. In his 1967 paper in Science, Willows reported recording from more than 50 of the cells and mapped their connections. In 1969 Willows and Hoyle described a group of electrically linked cells that decides whether a swim happens. In a 1973 series of papers, Willows, Derek Dorsett and Hoyle proposed a standard notation for the cells, related identified cells to the stages of the swim in a preliminary model, and showed that a brain isolated from the animal still generates the swim pattern. Peter Getting, a postdoctoral researcher with Willows, later defined the neurons of the circuit that generates this pattern.
significance: Paul Katz's 2007 Scholarpedia article places Willows's 1960s work "among the first" to show what single identified neurons do in producing behavior in any organism. A 2025 review by W. N. Frost and Katz credits the work, alongside 1967 nerve-cell maps in the sea hare *Aplysia* and in lobster, with opening the prospect of mapping whole circuits cell by cell. Both credits come from researchers in Willows's own scientific lineage. Independently, the OpenAlex database counts 153 citations of Willows's 1967 paper. His work was not an absolute first: the 2025 review records earlier stimulation of giant nerve fibers in squid and crayfish, identifiable *Aplysia* neurons from 1958 and, to its authors' knowledge, the first recordings from inside *Tritonia* cells in a 1964 Russian paper.
fhl_tie: The dissection took place at FHL, on a slug trawled from East Sound and kept in an FHL lab aquarium, and in an unpublished memoir Willows recalls spending two to three years there on thesis experiments mapping the brain. An article by W. N. Frost in FHL's Tide Bites dates the start of this work to summer 1964. Frost's 2025 review with Katz gives 1966, but that date conflicts with Willows's recordings, which were in print by April 1965. The 1964 date is therefore the better supported. Willows's 1965, 1967 and 1969 papers give University of Oregon addresses. He wrote his thesis in Eugene and recalls flying from there to FHL to fetch slugs or barnacles, so not every early experiment can be placed at FHL. The 1973 papers give FHL as the address for Willows and Dorsett and the University of Oregon for Hoyle. Where Getting carried out his later work on the circuit is not established.

title: The A-current and potassium channel diversity in nudibranch neurons
people: J. A. Connor, C. F. Stevens, S. H. Thompson, D. Walter, R. McKown; facilities credited to FHL directors R. L. Fernald and A. O. D. Willows
summary: A brief (transient) outward current in nerve cells, apparently carried by potassium, was named I-A, or the A-current, in work on San Juan Island nudibranchs (sea slugs). Hagiwara and colleagues in Tokyo had seen it in the mollusk *Onchidium* in 1961, and Neher described it in the snail *Helix* in 1971. In 1971 Connor and Stevens held isolated nerve-cell bodies of *Anisodoris* and other nudibranchs at set voltages (voltage clamp). They reported that the current could be told apart, at least by its behavior in their experiments, from the delayed potassium current called I-K. Connor and Stevens also wrote equations in the style of Hodgkin and Huxley's model of the nerve impulse, with the A-current included. The equations predicted firing rates well for the first interval between impulses, but rates that were too fast for later intervals. In 1977 Thompson used chemical blockers to separate potassium current in *Tritonia* neurons into three parts: a transient current and two delayed currents, one of which depends on calcium entry. The same year, Connor, Walter and McKown added a term for a transient potassium current to the Hodgkin-Huxley model, based on experiments with crab axons.
significance: In a 2021 account, Johnston credits the 1961 paper by Hagiwara and colleagues with the first description of the current, and Connor and Stevens with the name I-A, which has persisted. In a 2014 account, Jerng and Pfaffinger credit Connor and Stevens, alongside Neher's 1971 paper, with the current's detailed characterization. They also cite Connor and Stevens for the current's role in the timing and frequency of nerve impulses, and Thompson's 1977 paper for its sensitivities to the chemical blockers 4-aminopyridine and tetraethylammonium (TEA), which identify it. The citation database OpenAlex counts 1,095 citations for Connor and Stevens's 1971 paper on the current and 677 for Thompson's paper, and the Europe PMC database gives lower figures for both.
fhl_tie: All of Connor and Stevens's animals came from around San Juan Island, and the first of their three 1971 papers says that some experiments were done at FHL, in natural seawater. Most experiments used artificial seawater, which implies that most were done elsewhere, but the paper names no other place and assigns no data to either place. Their second paper, on the A-current, uses the same methods and thanks FHL director Fernald for the facilities. Their third paper does not name FHL. Thompson's *Tritonia* were trawled near FHL, and he thanks FHL director Willows for facilities there, but he does not say where the recordings were made. Connor and Stevens in 1971, and Thompson in 1977, give addresses at the University of Washington in Seattle, not FHL. Connor, Walter and McKown, with an address in Urbana, Illinois, thank Willows for FHL facilities during portions of their 1977 crab-axon study.

title: A network oscillator and intrinsic neuromodulation in the *Tritonia* swim circuit
people: Peter A. Getting, A. O. Dennis Willows, Paul S. Katz, William N. Frost, James M. Newcomb
summary: The sea slug *Tritonia* swims to escape, and the rhythm of that swim comes from the way its neurons connect. By the early 1980s Peter Getting, a former postdoc of Dennis Willows at FHL, and colleagues had identified the neurons of the central pattern generator, the circuit that makes the rhythm. None of them fires in bursts on its own, so the rhythm arises from their interactions, an arrangement called a network oscillator. A later rebuild of Getting's early realistic computer simulation, using measurements on rested nervous systems, did not generate the swim, which pointed to modulation by serotonin. Getting had described the dorsal swim interneurons, members of the circuit, as using serotonin to modulate other neurons. In 1994 Paul Katz, Getting and William Frost showed that these interneurons enhance the signals sent by another member of the circuit, an effect they called intrinsic neuromodulation. A 1996 paper by Frost and Katz identified DRI, a neuron Getting had inferred, as a command neuron in the strict sense, a single cell that drives the behavior. In the sea slug *Melibe*, the neurons corresponding to the dorsal swim interneurons modulate the swim circuit from outside it.
significance: Frost and Katz, who took part in this work, write in a review prompted by a January 2024 FHL conference that Getting's findings and ideas "revolutionized research on central pattern generators." Independently, Eve Marder's 2012 review in the journal Neuron calls Getting's 1989 review prescient. Marder cites Katz and Frost for the distinction between modulation from within a circuit (intrinsic) and from outside it (extrinsic), which she calls artificial at some level. She cites them alongside work on the sea hare *Aplysia* by Cropper, Weiss and colleagues, whose 1987 paper already spoke in its title of modulation intrinsic to the motor circuit. Golowasch's 2019 review treats the *Tritonia* escape-swim network as a model system for studying central pattern generators.
fhl_tie: Willows started *Tritonia* neuroscience at FHL, although a 1964 Russian paper had already reported recordings from the animal's neurons. Getting's 1973–74 papers on electrically coupled neurons (joined by direct electrical links) and Taghert and Willows's 1978 paper carry an FHL address. Getting's swim-circuit papers, by contrast, give Stanford as his address in 1976–77, Iowa and Stanford in 1981, and Iowa on the third paper of his four-part series, from 1983. No source places his simulation at FHL. Getting and Frost set up an experimental rig at FHL in summer 1986, and Frost recalls locating DRI there, without giving a date. Papers by Katz and Frost give a Houston address. Part of their 1995 study was done at FHL, and their 1995 and 1996 papers thank Willows for space at FHL. Whether their 1994 Nature paper with Getting contains FHL data is unknown. A Georgia State study of *Melibe* collected animals from the FHL dock and kept some at FHL.

title: Swimming circuits in the pteropod *Clione*
people: Richard A. Satterlie, Tigran P. Norekian, Andrew N. Spencer, Michael LaBarbera, Thomas J. Pirtle
summary: This work traced the nerve circuit that makes the pteropod *Clione limacina*, a swimming sea snail, beat its wings. In 1985 Richard Satterlie reported that at least four connecting nerve cells in the pedal ganglia, nerve centers of the foot, generate the swim rhythm, two each for upstroke and downstroke. By his account, the upstroke and downstroke pairs inhibit each other directly, and each apparently fires strongly when released from that inhibition, so the network keeps alternating without steady input or apparent feedback. Companion papers with Andrew Spencer and Michael LaBarbera described the wing muscles and reported a separate rhythm generator for each wing. In the 1990s Satterlie's work, much of it with Tigran Norekian, showed that neurons using the chemical signal serotonin speed swimming by separate routes: pedal cells make the wings contract more strongly, and cerebral cells, in the head, make them beat faster. Norekian and Satterlie also traced the neurons that push out the buccal cones, appendages used to capture prey, and proposed that motor neurons with opposite actions, firing together, drive the cones' fluid-driven inflation in 50 milliseconds.
significance: Independent reviews use the circuit as a standard small rhythm generator. A 2010 review by Selverston in Philosophical Transactions B gives *Clione* its own section, credits the 1985 papers by Arshavsky and colleagues and by Satterlie, and calls the circuit a hybrid of cell and network properties. A 2009 review by Goulding in Nature Reviews Neuroscience cites Satterlie for the two-part (half-center) oscillator in *Clione*. Priority does not belong to Satterlie's work. Arshavsky's Moscow group, citing two 1984 notes in a Russian journal, submitted in January 1984 a paper reporting that the circuit's neurons have a rhythm of their own, about seven months before Satterlie submitted his Science paper, which has 190 citations in the report's census.
fhl_tie: Satterlie was based at Arizona State and came to FHL in spring and summer, and *Clione* were dipped off the FHL dock and breakwater. His 1985 Science paper gives both Arizona State and FHL as addresses, but the sources do not establish where its recordings were made. The two companion papers say a significant portion of the work was done at FHL, though the first lists no FHL address. Later work was split between sites. A 1993 paper by Norekian and Satterlie reports behavioral and physiological experiments at FHL and work on body structure at Arizona State. A 1995 paper reports animals held in FHL seawater tanks and in refrigerators at Arizona State. Norekian's 1993 papers give FHL along with Arizona State as addresses. A 2021 paper by Thomas Pirtle and Satterlie again used animals from the breakwater.

title: Magnetic orientation in a sea slug
people: Kenneth J. Lohmann, A. O. Dennis Willows, Robert B. Pinter, Ion R. Popescu, John H. Wang, Shaun D. Cain, Galina A. Pavlova, Raymon M. Glantz
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: A sea slug can sense direction from Earth's magnetic field. Kenneth Lohmann, a doctoral student of FHL director Dennis Willows, reported this with Willows in 1987 for the species *Tritonia diomedea* (later renamed *Tritonia exsulans*). The slugs' preferred headings varied with the moon's phase. In 1991 Lohmann, Willows and Robert Pinter found that in partly dissected slugs a large nerve cell, Pd5, fired more about 6 to 16 minutes after a magnetic field of Earth's strength was rotated. Wang and colleagues (2003, 2004) found that the field also excited a cell type called Pd6 and inhibited one called Pd7. Popescu and Willows (1999) reported that signals in Pd5 ran from the brain out to the body, and the same was later found for Pd6 and Pd7. This direction of travel marks the six cells, a left and a right of each type, as likely to send signals outward rather than to detect the field. In field tests that Willows reported in 1999, slugs placed at different sites mostly moved in their original shoreward direction rather than the direction that was shoreward at each site, which suggested magnetic guidance. Pavlova, Glantz and Willows (2011) recorded responses in body nerves with the brain removed, which suggested that the receptors detecting the field are widely dispersed. Wyeth and colleagues (2021) say there is no definitive evidence of how slugs use the sense in nature.
significance: Wiltschko and Wiltschko's 2022 history of research on magnetic navigation names *Tritonia* as its mollusk example of response to magnetic field direction. Fenton and colleagues (2022) list the *Tritonia* recordings, with honeybee work, among studies that recorded nerve responses to magnetic fields in invertebrates, and they set these beside similar studies in vertebrates. Vertebrate recordings of this kind go back to 1984, according to Wang and colleagues (2003). Frost and Katz (2025), themselves *Tritonia* researchers, say the discovery inspired Lohmann to extend his work to other animals, including sea turtles, though his 1984–85 papers on magnetic cues in lobsters came earlier.
fhl_tie: Where the 1987 and 1991 experiments were done is not established. The 1987 paper lists both authors at FHL and University of Washington Zoology, and the 1991 paper lists only Pinter at FHL. Three later papers give FHL as the authors' address: Popescu and Willows (1999), Willows (1999), and Pavlova, Glantz and Willows (2011). The site of Willows's 1999 field tests is not established. The 2011 paper thanks FHL for animal care in all phases of the work. Wang and colleagues did most of their 2003 study in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on animals shipped there, with only tests using a single rotation of the magnetic field done at Friday Harbor. In their 2004 study and in a 2006 study led by Shaun Cain, Cain's address includes FHL, and his coauthors' addresses are at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. In the 2004 study, the animals were kept at FHL, no recording site is named, and funding came from a University of North Carolina fellowship and National Science Foundation grants to Lohmann. Lohmann's lobster and turtle papers, from Florida, Illinois and North Carolina, are not FHL work.

title: The contractile ring in dividing cells
people: Thomas E. Schroeder, David R. Burgess, Stephen A. Stricker, Joann J. Otto, John H. Henson, Charles B. Shuster
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Thomas Schroeder's electron microscopy measured the contractile ring, the band of filaments that pinches a dividing animal cell in two, and tied those filaments to muscle actin. In a 1972 paper on *Arbacia* sea urchin eggs, he found that the ring exists only briefly and eventually loses volume, and that the drug cytochalasin B removes the filaments and stops division within 60 seconds. In a 1973 paper on human HeLa cells, he reported that the ring filaments bind a fragment of muscle myosin in a way that marks them as close relatives of muscle actin. His later papers from FHL followed actin in eggs. With David Burgess in 1977 he studied sea urchin eggs. From 1981 to 1984, alone and with Stephen Stricker and Joann Otto, he studied the spikes that a hormone raises on immature eggs of the starfish *Pisaster ochraceus*. In 2017, John Henson, Charles Shuster and colleagues saw apparent head-to-head chains of myosin II, a motor protein, in sea urchin embryo rings at a late stage. They took this as support, in large spherical cells, for the purse-string model, in which the ring closes like a drawstring.
significance: Erfei Bi's 2010 piece in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology says the 1972 paper made four observations "that defined the field of cytokinesis," or cell division. Pollard's 2010 review calls the paper's electron microscopy classic. Credit is shared. Szollosi in 1970 and others had already reported filaments where the cell pinches in two, and Perry and colleagues reported actin-like filaments in the newt egg in 1971. A 2019 review by Pollard and O'Shaughnessy pairs Rappaport's measurement of the pinching force with Schroeder's identification of actin in the ring, citing his 1970 paper with a Stanford address and his 1973 paper with an FHL address. The same review cites the 2017 images by Henson and colleagues of myosin II filaments in sea urchin rings.
fhl_tie: Schroeder's FHL appointment began on June 1, 1971, when he took up year-round residence and set up an electron microscopy facility. The 1972 and 1973 papers give FHL as his address, but the 1972 paper reached the journal less than five months after that date, and where its eggs were obtained or sectioned is not established. His 1968 report of the filaments, from Seattle, and his 1970 paper, from Stanford, came before the appointment. The firmest FHL work came later: the papers of 1977 and of 1981 to 1984 give FHL addresses, with Joann Otto also giving Purdue on the 1984 paper, and the starfish for the 1981 paper were collected around the San Juan Archipelago. In the 2017 paper, John Henson of Dickinson and Charles Shuster of New Mexico State also give FHL as an address. The authors kept one of three urchin species at FHL and thank Billie Swalla for access to instruments and reagents there. University of Pennsylvania colleagues helped with the electron microscopy, and the paper does not say what was done at FHL.

title: Sperm chemotaxis across marine animals
people: Richard L. Miller, Kenneth R. King, Gary Freeman
summary: Richard L. Miller of Temple University extended his work on sperm that swim toward substances from eggs, a behavior called chemotaxis, to more marine groups, in papers that list FHL as an address. His 1979 papers on hydromedusae, the small jellyfish-like stage of hydrozoans, reported attraction that can be highly species-specific and described the attractants' chemical properties. In 1982 he identified closely similar sibling species in the *Sarsia tubulosa* complex at Friday Harbor. That year, with Gary Freeman, he reported that hydrozoan eggs can be fertilized only where the polar body forms, a small cell shed as the egg matures. Freeman restated this in 1996. With Kenneth R. King, Miller showed in 1983 that egg extract attracts sperm of the planktonic animal *Oikopleura dioica*. His 1985 paper demonstrated attraction in sea stars, sea cucumbers and brittle stars. Daily tests of FHL aquarium seawater in 1986, published in 1989, indicated that water carrying attractant at times entered the aquarium system.
significance: Credit for founding the field lies elsewhere. Kaupp's 2012 review gives the first report of chemotaxis in animal sperm to Lillie (1912) and says Miller's experiments of the late 1960s and 1970s firmly established it, citing his 1966 and 1970 papers and a 1985 chapter, none with an FHL address. Dan (1950), in Japan, separately inferred a specific attraction from sperm crowding at one end of the egg. Two FHL-linked papers kept being cited: 107 citations for the 1979 species-specificity paper and 136 for the 1985 paper in the report's census, and Yoshida's 2014 review lists both among its references.
fhl_tie: FHL was a second address for Miller, whose home remained Temple, and for Freeman, of the University of Texas. On the 1983 paper, Miller gave Temple alone and King gave UW Oceanography and FHL. Station work is documented for two papers: the 1983 paper collected *Oikopleura* as they drifted past the FHL dock and thanks FHL staff for hospitality during the authors' residence, and the 1989 paper tested seawater in the FHL aquarium system. The sources do not establish where the experiments in the 1979, 1982 and 1985 papers ran, though the 1982 title places its *Sarsia* at Friday Harbor. Miller's founding papers of 1966–1977 are not FHL's: they give Chicago and Woods Hole, Temple or Caltech.

title: Mitotic domains in the fly embryo
people: Victoria E. Foe, Garrett M. Odell
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: After 13 synchronized cycles of nuclear division, cells of a fruit fly (*Drosophila*) embryo break into at least 25 groups, called mitotic domains, each dividing on its own schedule, in the same positions and order in every embryo. Earlier workers had noted a complex division pattern at gastrulation, the stage when the embryo begins folding into layers. Victoria Foe and Garrett Odell reported the domains in May 1989, and Foe's detailed atlas followed that September. The domains appear about an hour into the 14th interphase, the pause between divisions. Foe timed events from time-lapse video and mapped the domains in stained, fixed embryos. Cells in some domains shared shape, direction of division and inward-folding behavior, which she read as an early sign of commitment to specific fates.
significance: Later *Drosophila* work uses the atlas as a reference. Blanchard and colleagues (2024) found that the division order they recorded by live imaging in five domains agreed with the sequence Foe identified in fixed samples. Camuglia and colleagues (2022) cite Edgar and O'Farrell (1989) alongside Foe for the pattern, so credit for it is not hers alone. The MacArthur Foundation named her a 1993 Fellow for the observation that embryo regions begin dividing at markedly different rates. Foe's atlas, published in the journal Development, has 440 citations in Crossref and 241 in Europe PMC.
fhl_tie: Foe gave FHL as her only address on both 1989 papers. NIH grant GM36263, which the Development paper credits, is listed in the town of Friday Harbor for fiscal 1985–1990 and at UW Seattle from fiscal 1991 in NIH grant records. The Development paper does not thank FHL or say where the embryos were raised or imaged. Odell, at UW Zoology in Seattle, built a temperature controller and wrote a timing program for the atlas. John Minden's movies corrected one domain's assignment. The only stated use of FHL's labs is for part of an earlier study on another topic, Foe and Alberts (1985). The Mills and Hermans FHL timeline dates her residence from about 2000 and is silent on the 1980s.

title: Center for Cell Dynamics: how embryo cells polarize and divide
people: Garrett Odell, Victoria Foe, Edwin Munro, George von Dassow, Kristin Sherrard, William Bement, Hélène Benink, Brian Burkel, Jeremy Nance, James Priess, François Robin, Patrick Lemaire
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: The Center for Cell Dynamics, an NIH center led by Garrett Odell at FHL from 2002 to about 2010, paired live embryo microscopy with computer models of cells. In January 2002, before the center began, Edwin Munro and Odell described how the sea squirt notochord, the embryo's support rod, forms. In 2004 Munro, Jeremy Nance and James Priess reported that the contractile actin-myosin layer of the one-cell *Caenorhabditis elegans* worm embryo flows and appears to carry with it PAR proteins, which set up the embryo's front and back. In 2005 William Bement, Hélène Benink and George von Dassow reported a precise zone of active RhoA, a signaling protein, directed by microtubules (fibers of the cell's internal skeleton), before division in echinoderm (sea urchin group) and frog embryos. In 2007 Brian Burkel, von Dassow and Bement described utrophin-based probes that mark actin in living cells. In 2008 Victoria Foe and von Dassow tested how microtubules determine where myosin is activated in echinoderm eggs, and Odell and Foe simulated that mechanism on a computer. In 2010 Kristin Sherrard, Munro and colleagues in Marseille analyzed how sea squirt embryos fold inward.
significance: Gubieda and colleagues (2020) call Munro's 2004 paper seminal and credit Munro and co-workers with first describing the transport of PAR proteins by the flow, in a sentence that also cites papers by Cheeks and colleagues (2004) and Cuenca and colleagues (2003). They credit Hird and White (1993) with first measuring the flow. Basant and Glotzer (2018) cite Bement's 2005 paper, as one of three references, for zones of active RhoA where cells pinch in two. Belin and colleagues (2014) list utrophin domains among commonly used live actin probes while documenting the probes' biases. Jiang and Smith (2007) call Munro and Odell's notochord papers seminal.
fhl_tie: The center and its staff were at FHL. Both 2008 papers give a Friday Harbor address for their authors, and the experimental one used urchins and sand dollars from near San Juan Island, Eastsound and Clallam Bay. In the 2004 paper Munro's address was Friday Harbor, Nance and Priess were in Seattle, and where the imaging was done is not established. The 2005 and 2007 papers give the center as von Dassow's address and both the center and Wisconsin as Bement's, with correspondence to Wisconsin. Benink and Burkel were at Wisconsin, and the methods of the 2005 paper do not name FHL. The 2010 paper gives the center as Sherrard's and Munro's address, shares the work with colleagues in Marseille and thanks Roscoff, France, for animals. The 2002 papers predate the center and list Seattle, though the OpenAlex database also records Friday Harbor for Munro. Where that work was done is not established.

title: Electrical control of polarity in *Obelia*
people: E. J. (Elmer Julius) Lund; H. F. Rosene (coauthor, 1930)
summary: E. J. Lund showed that electric current could control which end of a cut stem regrows (its polarity) in *Obelia*, a small colonial hydroid related to jellyfish, and that living stems carry their own electrical potential. He built on electrical potentials that Mathews had found in other hydroids in 1903 and on his own 1917 regeneration work on the single-celled *Bursaria*. In 1921 a current blocked the polyp (feeding head) at the end facing the cathode (negative electrode), while the end facing the anode (positive) regrew. In 1922 he used a current meter to show a potential along the stems that depended on living tissue and was greatest at the growing tip. By 1924 he had found that the block was reversible and that a current about one-tenth as strong, applied across the stem, bent growth toward the anode. Cyanide, ether and chloroform reversibly reduced the potential. Later papers tie such potentials to cell oxidation, the cell's use of oxygen, and measure them in Douglas fir. The book Bioelectric Fields and Growth (University of Texas Press, 1947) gathered this program of work.
significance: Jaffe and Nuccitelli (1977) rank Lund's studies as the most significant and influential early work on electric fields in development, after Mathews had measured potentials along regenerating hydroids in 1903 and proposed that they might influence growth. Rose (1970) credits Lund's 1921 paper with clearly demonstrating that an electric field applied from outside determines the polarity of regeneration, while noting that Mathews had mentioned a preliminary experiment with applied current. Borgens, Vanable and Jaffe (1979) call Lund a "remarkable pioneer" but caution that his stems were measured in moist air, so the direction of current he reported may be valid while its size cannot be determined from his published data.
fhl_tie: Lund held posts at the University of Minnesota and then the University of Texas, and he taught General Physiology at the Puget Sound Biological Station (FHL) in the summers of 1920 and 1921. His 1921 paper gives the station's laboratory as its only marine address and describes colonies taken from the laboratory float and kept in flowing seawater. That places his first current experiments at the station only by inference, since no source names the place outright. His later journal papers on *Obelia*, a 1928 paper on cell oxidation and his Douglas fir papers list the station beside his home university through 1931, though an address alone does not show where the work was done. Notes from 1923 and 1924 give only a Minnesota address, a 1925 note on cyanide gives a Naples and Minnesota address, and the 1947 book came from Texas, so the station cannot be credited with the whole program.

title: Changing RNA populations in sea urchin embryos
people: Arthur H. Whiteley, Brian J. McCarthy, Helen R. Whiteley, Michael A. Harkey, Jean J. Comita, John W. Brookbank, Albert L. Bolst, J. B. Litchfield, Joram Piatigorsky, Shigeki Mizuno, Y. R. Lee
summary: Arthur Whiteley's group compared the RNA of sea urchin eggs and embryos and concluded that eggs already hold messenger RNA, which carries a gene's instructions for making protein. From the early 1950s the group measured respiration, DNA, the enzyme urease and phosphate uptake in purple sea urchin embryos; Albert Tyler proposed the 1953 study comparing DNA with respiration. In 1966 Whiteley, Brian McCarthy and Helen Whiteley let unlabeled RNA from eggs, embryos and adult tissues compete with labeled RNA from a later stage, the prism, for binding to matching DNA, a method called hybridization. Egg RNA could not be told apart from RNA of the hollow-ball blastula stage. RNA from the gastrula, the stage when the gut forms, nearly matched prism RNA, and RNA from adult tissues competed weakly. In 1975 the group published two papers on RNA copied from repeated DNA sequences. In 1980 Michael Harkey and Whiteley isolated primary mesenchyme cells, which build the skeleton, from early gastrulae at 95 percent purity, and over 90 percent of the cells formed skeletal spicules in culture.
significance: In a 1966 Harvard study, Glisin, Glisin and Doty called their work complementary to the Whiteley paper of the same year. They noted that the Whiteley paper used too little labeled RNA to come near filling the DNA's binding sites, and argued from both studies that between blastula and gastrula some copying of DNA into RNA turns off and other copying turns on. Skoultchi and Gross (1973), citing both papers, wrote that hybridization had shown information-carrying RNA sequences in eggs but given no direct evidence for specific maternal messenger RNAs, those the mother stores in the egg. Stumpp and colleagues (2012) used Harkey and Whiteley's 1980 protocol to remove cells from larvae. Moreno and colleagues (2019) credit Okazaki (1975) with the first large-scale isolation and culture of micromeres, small cells of the early embryo, work that preceded the 1980 study of gastrula cells.
fhl_tie: Arthur Whiteley taught from 1947 at the University of Washington in Seattle, where Brian McCarthy and Helen Whiteley were colleagues. FHL's own accounts say he set up a summer laboratory at FHL, worked "at FHL and Seattle" and combined efforts at FHL with Helen Whiteley. Papers from 1953 to 1980 give the Zoology department and FHL as the authors' address, and the eggs for the 1953 study came from San Juan Island. The 1966 paper gives Seattle departments and FHL as addresses and names no place of work, so how the laboratory work was divided is not established. FHL's centennial timeline, compiled with Whiteley's help, credits his work with the "first published use" of DNA-RNA hybridization on embryonic events, but it names no paper. The 1966 paper cites earlier work by Gross and colleagues (1965) on RNA-DNA binding during the formation of egg cells, and by Denis (1964), who reached a similar conclusion in the frog *Xenopus*. The paper by Glisin, Glisin and Doty followed months later, so "first" remains the timeline's claim.

title: Development and larvae of sipunculan worms
people: Mary E. Rice; Robert L. Fernald (doctoral advisor); Paul Illg (thanked in the 1973 monograph)
summary: Mary E. Rice traced how sipunculans, or peanut worms, develop from the egg in three San Juan Archipelago species, and described the larvae of two. Earlier studies of sipunculan development include those by Selenka in 1875 and Gerould in 1906. Rice was at the University of Washington from 1961 and chose sipunculans when her doctoral advisor, Robert Fernald, had each student pick an invertebrate group. Her 1967 paper covered breeding, eggs and early cell divisions. *Themiste pyroides* hatches directly as a crawling worm. *Phascolosoma agassizii* and *Golfingia pugettensis* pass from a swimming larva (a trochophore) to a second larva living both near the seabed and in open water, feeding on plankton in the first species and on yolk in the second. By her later account, the 1967 paper set out four developmental patterns for sipunculans as a whole and defined the pelagosphera, as this second larva is called. Mueller had recognized such larvae in 1850. Her 1973 Smithsonian monograph described that larva's anatomy, behavior and tissue development in *P. agassizii*. Her 1976 review recognizes four patterns of development.
significance: An independent 2011 study by Kristof and colleagues cites Rice's 1967 paper for the direct development of *T. pyroides*, without a swimming larva, in the northeast Pacific. Grzimek's Animal Life Encyclopedia describes four developmental modes and lists her 1976 review among its references, but it does not credit the scheme to her. The author of that entry, Anja Schulze, coauthored publications with Rice. The St. Petersburg Society of Naturalists gave Rice its 2019 Kovalevsky Medal. Billie Swalla's tribute to Rice says the medal was for the comparative embryology, development and evolution of sipunculans. The medal honors a wider career, mostly at the Smithsonian, not the FHL work alone.
fhl_tie: FHL's newsletter says Rice did most of her doctoral dissertation research there under Fernald, earning her PhD in 1966, and that she was among the first graduate students to work there through the winter. The 1967 paper gives FHL, the University of Washington's zoology department and the Smithsonian as affiliations, and the sources do not establish where its laboratory work was done. The 1973 monograph, part of her dissertation, thanks Fernald, as FHL's director, for the use of FHL facilities, but its methods section does not name where the larvae were reared. The adult worms for that work came from the San Juan Archipelago and Vancouver Island. The 1976 review, which gives only a Smithsonian address, and her work on Gulf Stream larvae belong to her later Smithsonian career, during which she returned to FHL for summer research.

title: Experimental embryology of body axes
people: Gary Freeman, Ellis B. Ridgway
summary: Gary Freeman's experiments on marine embryos tied the main body axis of comb jellies and hydrozoans (jellyfish and polyps) to the site of first cleavage, the egg's first division. His 1977 study made this link for the comb jelly's oral-aboral (mouth-to-far-end) axis. In his 1981 papers on hydrozoans, isolated parts of embryos formed normal planulae (swimming larvae) that kept the original axis. In centrifuged eggs whose first cleavage began away from the polar body site, where a small cell leaves the egg, the posterior (oral) pole formed at the cleavage site. When he suppressed first cleavage, two division furrows formed together at the next division, and furrows far enough apart gave two-tailed planulae. In 1987 and 1990, he and Ellis Ridgway tracked calcium in hydrozoan eggs and larvae through the animals' own light-giving proteins. Calcium channels appeared to become active around first cleavage, and blocking the calcium pulses set off by bacteria or cesium also blocked metamorphosis. In 1991 and 1993 he isolated regions of *Phoronis* (horseshoe worm) and *Terebratalia* (lamp shell) embryos to time when each region's fate is set.
significance: Peron, Houliston and Leclère (2021) say that the jellyfish *Clytia gregaria*, used extensively by Freeman, "played an important part in the history of cnidarian experimental embryology" (cnidarians include jellyfish). Fischer et al. (2014) cite him for the finding that first cleavage sets the comb jelly axis. Uveira et al. (2025) call his manipulations classic and credit them with the concept of global polarity (an overall directional organization across the whole embryo). In their reply to reviewers, the same authors call the first-cleavage result a milestone and some of his interpretations misleading. They also note that Freeman revisited Georges Teissier's 1931 experiments, and that the maternal determinants (axis-setting substances in the egg) that Freeman's view stood against were later shown in *Clytia*.
fhl_tie: Freeman was based at the University of Texas, not at FHL, and Ridgway at the Medical College of Virginia. All nine cited papers give an FHL address, as do other papers of his from 1976 to 2009. A 1983 paper on direct development in hydrozoans used *Aglantha* and *Nanomia*, collected from the FHL dock, and thanks the FHL director for facilitating the work there. The 1993 paper on *Terebratalia* metamorphosis used animals from near San Juan Island and thanks FHL for its hospitality. For the other seven, including the 1977 and 1981 axis studies, the address is the only evidence of work at FHL. Freeman also co-taught Comparative Invertebrate Embryology at FHL in summer 1981. A separate 1976 comb jelly study gives Texas and Woods Hole as its addresses, and a 1992 paper and the 2004 review that named global polarity give only Texas. The jellyfish *Clytia hemisphaerica*, a different species from Freeman's, was developed as a laboratory model at Villefranche and Paris from 2002.

title: Changing roles of homeobox genes in echinoderm evolution
people: Christopher J. Lowe and Gregory A. Wray; D. Willows, R. Strathmann and FHL staff thanked for facilities
summary: In 1997, Christopher Lowe and Gregory Wray reported that three body-patterning homeobox genes are used in varied ways in echinoderms (sea urchins, sea stars and their relatives). Using antibodies, they mapped where the Distal-less, Engrailed and Orthodenticle proteins appear in larvae and juveniles from four of the five living classes of echinoderms, although they mapped Engrailed only in the brittle star *Amphipholis squamata*. All three proteins formed fivefold radial patterns as the adult body developed, mostly in structures found only in echinoderms, such as tube feet. Other patterns were limited to one class. An earlier paper had already reported Distal-less in sea urchin tube feet and spines. Without testing what the genes do, Lowe and Wray inferred from these patterns that the genes had been recruited to different roles, some more than 450 million years ago and others later. They also inferred that these genes, known for changing little between arthropods and chordates, are flexible in how they are used.
significance: In a News and Views commentary in the same issue of Nature, Eric Davidson used Lowe and Wray's paper to argue that regulatory genes are recruited to new roles class by class, and that a gene's pattern of activity alone cannot establish homology (shared evolutionary origin) between distant animals. A 2023 paper in Nature by Formery and colleagues, with Lowe as a coauthor, cited the 1997 paper as a proposal of co-option, the reuse of existing genes for new roles. Studying a much larger set of genes in a sea star, they favored modification of an ancestral program that patterns the body axis, while leaving co-option possible. The report's census counts 209 citations of the 1997 paper.
fhl_tie: The tie to FHL is partial. Adult animals were collected around San Juan Island, and the acknowledgments of Lowe and Wray's paper thank D. Willows, R. Strathmann and FHL staff for facilities. FHL's own 2002 review calls the work "a study at FHL," but that is FHL's own account, not an independent one. The authors gave their address as the State University of New York, Stony Brook, and other laboratories shared the probes and primers used to detect and copy genes. The paper does not say where the animals were reared or where the staining, cloning or sequencing took place, so which steps used FHL's facilities is not documented. Wray had given an FHL address on papers from 1991–92 and is listed as co-teaching FHL's embryology course in 1994 and 1996, but no source links that address or that teaching to this study.

title: Evolution of tunicates and hemichordates
people: Billie J. Swalla, Brad Davidson, Liyun Zeng, Noa Shenkar, Johanna Taylor Cannon, Kenneth M. Halanych
summary: Billie Swalla and colleagues studied how tunicates and hemichordates, invertebrate relatives of vertebrates, develop and how they are related. In a 2002 paper, Brad Davidson and Swalla isolated gene transcripts from metamorphosing *Boltenia villosa*, a sea squirt or ascidian (a kind of tunicate), and a significant share matched innate immune genes. In a 2005 review of the family tree of these groups, Liyun Zeng and Swalla argued that tunicates should be a separate phylum and raised the possibility of a colonial tunicate ancestor. Johanna Taylor Cannon, a doctoral student in Kenneth Halanych's group at Auburn University, worked with Swalla to place deep-sea acorn worms on the hemichordate family tree, in a paper published in 2009. A 2011 paper by Noa Shenkar and Swalla compiled 2,815 described ascidian species from the literature and the World Register of Marine Species, listing 64 non-indigenous ones. A 2014 analysis of 185 genes by Cannon and colleagues, including Swalla, found acorn worms and pterobranchs (small tube-dwelling hemichordates) to be separate groups, unlike the tree in the 2009 paper.
significance: Recognition rests on citations and a career award, not one result. The 2011 paper by Shenkar and Swalla has 286 citations in the report's census. A 2018 review by Irie, Satoh and Kuratani calls largely unchallenged the view that chordates, the larger group that includes vertebrates and tunicates, divide into three subphyla, with tunicates as one. It names two Swalla papers, from 2000 and 2005, among the few that suggested a tunicate phylum. A 2015 review by Hejnol and Lowe cites the 2014 analysis for the two hemichordate groups, and a 2016 paper by Song and colleagues cites the 2002 paper for immune genes at metamorphosis. The Society for Developmental Biology gave Swalla its 2025 Lifetime Achievement Award for her whole career.
fhl_tie: The sources place only part of this work at FHL. Swalla joined the University of Washington in 1999. Her papers carry an FHL address from 2001, usually beside a Seattle one, and she led FHL as acting or interim director from 2012 and director from 2014 to 2019. The firmest tie is the 2002 study, which states that many of its experiments were conducted at FHL, with *Boltenia* harvested there. The other links are looser. The 2005 and 2009 papers list FHL among several addresses, and the only link in the 2011 literature and database review is Swalla's FHL address. The 2014 analysis was led from Auburn, with Cannon on an FHL fellowship and FHL among the stations that helped collect specimens. Swalla's 2008 review with A. B. Smith gives a Seattle address and does not name FHL, and her 2000 family-tree papers list Vanderbilt and Seattle rather than FHL.

title: Evolution of insect metamorphosis
people: James W. Truman, Lynn M. Riddiford, Michelle Herko, Helen Chea
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: James Truman and Lynn Riddiford argued that complete metamorphosis, the larva-pupa-adult life cycle whose origin had long been disputed, evolved in steps, and identified the gene chinmo as the larval part of the three-gene system behind it in the fruit fly *Drosophila*. Reviews in 2019 proposed that flight favored differences between young and adult insects, and that altered embryo development then produced the larva. Truman and Riddiford's joint review supported Berlese's century-old idea of how the larva arose. In 2022 they used gene silencing to remove Chinmo from parts of the larva. The genes broad and E93 then came on early, and the tissue shifted toward metamorphic functions. They concluded that Chinmo (larva), Broad (pupa) and E93 (adult) inhibit one another, with no experimental evidence for two of those links. In the firebrat *Thermobia domestica*, a wingless insect without metamorphosis, juvenile hormone, known for its part in metamorphosis, appeared late in embryo development, and suppressing it impaired differentiation and hatching.
significance: Stuart Reynolds's 2022 PNAS commentary credits Truman and Riddiford with finding in chinmo the larval gene missing from the three-gene scheme Williams and Kafatos proposed about 50 years earlier, and cautions that the evolutionary reading rests on two species. Reynolds reviewed the paper, so his account is not fully separate from it. Other labs reported the larval role in the beetle *Tribolium* and the moth *Spodoptera* and precocious metamorphosis after chinmo silencing in a cockroach (Chafino et al. 2023; Escudero et al. 2025). Xavier Belles's 2023 eLife commentary presented the firebrat result as a clue to how metamorphosis evolved.
fhl_tie: Truman and Riddiford taught FHL apprenticeships on arthropods in 2003, 2005 and 2007 and set up their laboratory there in 2016. Helen Chea's firebrat pilot data came from a 2003 FHL course. Their 2022 paper gives only an FHL address and the firebrat paper lists FHL for three authors, but neither says where bench work was done. Much groundwork came from elsewhere. Their 1999 hypothesis on the origins of metamorphosis and Riddiford's work on the gene Broad give Seattle addresses, Zhu and colleagues isolated chinmo in 2006, a 2017 report from Oregon prompted testing it, and part of the work drew on sabbaticals at Australian National University and Cambridge. FHL's bibliographies list 1991 and 2006 Truman papers with Seattle addresses and no word on station work.

title: The ctenophore genome and the origin of nervous systems
people: Leonid L. Moroz, Billie J. Swalla, Andreas Heyland, Andrea B. Kohn, Claudia E. Mills, Tigran P. Norekian, Kevin M. Kocot, Kenneth M. Halanych, Evgeny I. Rogaev, David O. Girardo, Joshua J. Swore, Alexander Fodor, Rachel Sanford, Rebecca Bruders, Mathew R. Citarella
summary: In 2014 a team led by Leonid Moroz reported a draft genome of the Pacific sea gooseberry *Pleurobrachia bachei*, a comb jelly (ctenophore), and proposed that nervous systems, and possibly the way cells become muscle, evolved independently more than once. A 2008 study by Dunn and colleagues had suggested ctenophores were the earliest branch of the animal tree, and later authors credit it as the first to do so. University of Washington (UW) students in apprenticeships at FHL in 2008, 2010 and 2012 collected animals and embryos, compiled gene lists, did bioinformatics (computer analysis of genetic data) and ran lab experiments. The 2014 paper reported that many neuron-specific genes of bilaterians (insects, vertebrates and their relatives) and classical pathways for chemical transmitters, the signals neurons send, were absent or not expressed in neurons. The authors also placed ctenophores as the earliest branch, though support for that placement weakened within the paper itself when more ctenophore species were sampled, and the most conserved genes left the branching order unresolved.
significance: Whether ctenophores are the earliest branch is disputed. Pisani and colleagues (2015) wrote that the idea was questioned soon after the 2008 study, then revived by studies including the 2014 paper and the genome of another comb jelly, *Mnemiopsis*, and they called it an artifact of inadequate methods. Simion and colleagues (2017) supported sponges as earliest. Kenneth Halanych (2015), a coauthor of the 2014 paper, defended the placement, and Schultz and colleagues (2023) supported it with ancient groupings of genes on chromosomes. Independent origin is also contested: King and Rokas (2017) report no consensus on the placement and consider a rudimentary nervous system in the shared ancestor more likely, and Schultz and colleagues leave open either separate origins of neurons or their loss in sponges.
fhl_tie: Six species, including *Pleurobrachia*, were collected at FHL, and the 2014 paper thanks FHL for facilities during collection and for the Marine Genomics apprenticeships. A 2014 UW News story says the findings rest in part on analysis and work done at FHL, including student research. Seven of the 36 authors list an FHL address, and only Billie Swalla and Claudia Mills list it as their sole address. Moroz, of the Whitney Laboratory in Florida, conceived and led the work, and 15 authors list a Whitney address. Phylogenomics (building evolutionary trees from many genes) is credited to Kevin Kocot and Kenneth Halanych of Auburn University. Neither the paper's main text nor the UW News story places sequencing at FHL. FHL's part rests on its staff, on collecting and on the apprenticeships, not on leading the work.

title: Evolution of feeding larvae, brooding and the single-cell stage
people: Richard R. Strathmann, Megumi F. Strathmann, Richard K. Grosberg, Lucienne Fenaux
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Richard Strathmann studied why related marine animals have feeding larvae, nonfeeding larvae or brooded young, and why many-celled life keeps a single-cell stage. His 1975 paper, following work on egg size by Thorson (1950) and Vance (1973), tied feeding capacity in larvae of sea urchins and their relatives to the length of the ciliated band, a strip of beating hairs, and argued that losing a feeding stage is usually irreversible. His 1978 and 1985 papers took the question across marine invertebrates. In 1982 he and Megumi Strathmann reviewed the trend toward more brood care in smaller adults and found that no one explanation fit every case. Experiments they published with Lucienne Fenaux in 1992 suggested that food-driven changes in sea urchin larvae, described in 1988 reports, contribute to the shift to nonfeeding larvae. Two reviews with Richard Grosberg as first author (1998, 2007) stressed conflict among cell lineages and the single-cell bottleneck, when a new individual starts from one cell. A 2002 paper with six coauthors argued that wide larval dispersal may be an incidental byproduct of larvae moving from the parents' habitat into open water and back.
significance: Collin et al. (2021) cite Strathmann's 1978 papers for the view that regaining feeding larvae is uncommon or virtually impossible, then report calyptraeid snails whose retained larval feeding structures lower the barrier to regaining feeding. Sewell (1994), working at Bamfield Marine Station, used the hypotheses of the 1982 review to frame a study of a small brooding sea cucumber, found no size-related limit on brood size, and credited Chia (1974) and Heath (1977) for related ideas. Herron et al. (2022) call the 2007 review's estimate of "at least 25" origins of multicellularity very likely a serious underestimate. Three former PhD students of Strathmann introduced a 2010 symposium marking his contributions.
fhl_tie: Strathmann took FHL summer classes from 1964 and was resident associate director from 1973 to 2008, and FHL's timeline says his larval research drew students and postdocs there. Author addresses name FHL on all eight papers named above, but an address does not show where work was done, and four of the papers are reviews (1982, 1985, 1998, 2007). Methods sections of other papers, from 1989 and 1993, say larvae were reared at FHL, and a 1999 paper says adults were collected in front of the station. Where the 1992 experiments were done is not established, and the 2002 paper does not say its work was done at FHL. A 1994 food-limitation study, with Lucienne Fenaux of Villefranche as first author, used a northwest Mediterranean sea urchin. Strathmann's CV lists 1980–81 Guggenheim research at the Smithsonian and the Marine Biological Association UK.

title: Experiments on larval form, feeding and predation
people: Richard R. Strathmann, Megumi F. Strathmann, Michael W. Hart, Isabelle F. Boidron-Metairon, Lucienne Fenaux, Barry Sinervo, Larry R. McEdward, Richard B. Emlet, J. Timothy Pennington, Fu-Shiang Chia, Dawn Vaughn, Kathryn A. McDonald
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: These experiments measured how larval form affects feeding, swimming and survival. Emlet, in papers from 1982 to 1990, measured skeletal stiffness, drag and the flow of water around larvae. Pennington and Chia (1985) offered seven predators abalone larvae either before torsion, the twisting of a snail's body during development, or after its first 90 degrees. One predator ate significantly fewer of the twisted larvae and another ate significantly more, so the results did not support Garstang's idea that torsion defends larvae. Sinervo and McEdward (1988) separated the cells of early sea urchin embryos to reduce the effective egg size, and the larvae developed at rates like those of a species with smaller eggs. Boidron-Metairon (1988) and Strathmann and colleagues (1992) found that sand dollar and sea urchin larvae grew longer arms and feeding bands when food was scarce. Hart and Strathmann (1994) showed that the longer bands raised peak feeding rates but only partly made up for the shortage. Vaughn and Strathmann (2008) reported that larvae of the sand dollar *Dendraster excentricus* clone themselves, producing smaller larvae, when exposed to fish mucus, a predator cue. Vaughn (2010) inferred cloning from larval density, size, stage and some budding, and found that fish ate more uncloned siblings than clones. McDonald and Vaughn (2010) found that more food gave dense cultures of smaller larvae, which is consistent with cloning.
significance: Soars and colleagues at the University of Sydney (2009), citing these arm-growth papers and others, call such growth one of the most familiar examples of form changing with conditions, though they conclude it is not universal. Nilsson and Pernet (2022) call it a major focus of larval biology for three decades. They report a challenge to the result, over the density at which larvae were reared, that their replication only partly resolves; their paper is not wholly independent of FHL, since Pernet has papers with FHL addresses. Trackenberg and colleagues (2020), who worked partly at FHL, cite Sinervo and McEdward among others for the pattern that smaller urchin embryos develop more slowly, which the two sea stars they studied did not clearly follow. The torsion test and Emlet's mechanical measurements have smaller records of citation and later use. Dolmatov (2014), writing from Russia, calls larval cloning a way of avoiding predation.
fhl_tie: The sources place only some of this work at FHL. Pennington's University of Alberta dissertation states that all its research was done at FHL, including its studies of torsion, of larval bristles as a defense against predators, and of the vertical migration of sand dollar larvae, though the migration study sampled plankton in East Sound on Orcas Island. The journal papers from that research give addresses at Alberta or the University of Washington. Emlet's 1982 and 1990 papers and Hart's 1991 paper thank FHL for facilities and used some local animals; Emlet's 1990 paper also gives a Berkeley address. Pennington and Strathmann (1990) compared four classes of larvae at FHL and removed larval skeletons at Kewalo Marine Laboratory in Hawaii. Boidron-Metairon, of the University of Puerto Rico, worked with the sand dollar *Dendraster* at FHL, according to an abstract of the 1988 paper; where that paper's other species, the sea urchin *Lytechinus*, was reared is not established. The other papers, including those on cloning, give FHL as an address or name it as a supporter, and where their work was done is not established; Strathmann and colleagues (1992) also give an address in Villefranche, France.

title: Rafting by brooding invertebrates and sand dollar settlement near adults
people: Raymond C. Highsmith
summary: Raymond Highsmith found that sand dollar larvae prefer to settle in sand from adult beds, and that small brooding invertebrates, which keep their young with them and have no swimming larvae, can float and ride on drifting algae. His 1982 study of the sand dollar *Dendraster excentricus* linked the larvae's preference to a chemical cue that adults produce and the sand holds, possibly a small peptide (a short chain of amino acids). A tube-building tanaid (a small crustacean), *Leptochelia dubia*, reduced the survival of young sand dollars that had just metamorphosed from larvae, and adults reworking the sand excluded that predator from the beds. His 1985 paper dealt with rafting, the spread of animals on floating material, which was widely assumed but little measured. He set brooding tanaids, amphipods (also crustaceans) and bivalves on the water surface in containers and counted them as they resubmerged. Small individuals floated for hours to days, and most tanaids survived. Samples of drifting algae from Mitchell Bay carried brooding animals. He concluded that the data showed a potential for dispersal and did not prove that dispersal happens.
significance: Rodriguez, Ojeda and Inestrosa (1993), in a review of invertebrate settlement, cite Highsmith's 1982 paper for an adult-produced cue that keeps settling larvae in adult beds and away from predators. They cite it alongside Burke (1984), whose extract of sand from beds of the same species yielded a small peptide, and they list settlement induced by adults in other animal groups going back to Knight-Jones (1953). The standing of Highsmith's 1985 paper rests on continuing citation, with 283 citations in this report's census of FHL publications. Nikula and colleagues (2010) cite it, with older work, when they say that rafting is not a new idea. Millan-Medina and colleagues (2024) cite it while arguing that rafting's potential for present-day genetic exchange between populations may be overestimated.
fhl_tie: The methods section of the 1985 paper places the research at FHL in May–August 1982 and July–August 1984, with animals from False Bay and drift samples from Mitchell Bay and Beaverton Cove. An FHL Postdoctoral Fellowship and the University of Alaska's Institute of Marine Science supported the work, and Highsmith had moved to Alaska by the time the paper appeared. The 1982 Ecology paper gives an FHL address for Highsmith, and a 2019 FHL student report describes it as research done at FHL, but the sources do not establish where its experiments ran. His 1982 review of coral fragmentation is not FHL work: it rests on field data from Panama and names FHL only as his address when it was published.

title: Shelford and Powers's gradient-tank experiments on marine fishes
people: Victor E. Shelford, Edwin B. Powers
summary: Victor Shelford and Edwin Powers tested how herring and other marine fishes react to dissolved gases, acidity and temperature, using tanks in which the water changed gradually from one end to the other. In summer 1914 Shelford ran young Pacific herring and humpback salmon through such a tank at the Friday Harbor station and charted each fish's path. With Powers he reported in 1915 that herring turned back from hydrogen sulfide and carbon dioxide, responded to acidity more than salinity, and appeared to detect temperature differences of 0.2 °C. Shelford's 1918 tests for an acid sewage-treatment process had herring separating pH 8.1 from 8.2, a small step on the acidity scale, in a few runs. In 1918 and 1919 Powers took more than 500 seawater samples and found herring and salmon smolts (young salmon ready for the sea) at or near the pH they chose in the tank. Bottom and plant-dwelling fishes showed no such selection. In 1921 he tested how pH affected the oxygen herring could extract.
significance: Chidester's 1924 review of fish migration credited Shelford and Powers with showing that herring detect 0.2 °C and respond to acidity more than salinity. Sundin's 2023 review of ocean acidification lists their 1915 paper among the earliest work on fish reactions to carbon dioxide, alongside two 1913 studies. The idea that gradients steer migration stayed unproven. Powers himself denied that pH or carbon dioxide controls all fishes. Doudoroff (1938) called gradient-based accounts of migration speculative, in general terms without naming these authors, and reported that Shelford by 1929 saw the method as measuring acclimation more than habitat preference.
fhl_tie: The station was the site of the 1914 herring work, the 1918 acid tests, Powers's 1918–1919 seawater and gradient work, and his 1921 Pacific herring respiration tests. Shelford (Chicago, then Illinois) and Powers (Colorado College, then Nebraska) came in summers to teach or do research. The station paid for all of the 1918 tests and all but $125 of the 1914 work. Shelford and Allee had already published gradient experiments on fishes in 1913. The Atlantic-species half of Powers's 1922 respiration paper was done at Woods Hole in 1920. Shelford's 1919 article was written for the Illinois Natural History Survey and largely concerns fresh waters, drawing on the station work for its marine section.

title: Bottom and shore animal communities of the San Juans
people: Victor E. Shelford, E. D. Towler, A. O. Weese, Lucile A. Rice, D. I. Rasmussen, Archie MacLean, H. C. Markus, Leonard G. Worley, Nettie M. Wismer, John H. Swanson
summary: Surveys of 1922–1930 mapped the animal communities of the shores and sea floor around the San Juan Islands, defining each community by its dominant species rather than its habitat. Victor Shelford, with E. D. Towler of La Grande High School, surveyed San Juan Channel mainly in summer 1922, adding Shelford's records since 1914. Drawing on Clements's plant-community principles and Petersen's Danish bottom work, their 1925 paper named the *Balanus*-*Littorina*, *Macoma* and *Strongylocentrotus*-*Argobuccinum* communities and a pelagic (open-water) one, and found no basis for Forbes's Laminarian (kelp) belt as an animal community. Barnacle papers by Towler, Rice, Worley and Shelford followed in 1930. A 1935 monograph widened the area from about 75 to 1000 square kilometers, described a fourth bottom community, the *Pandora*-*Yoldia* biome, on mud in protected bays, and gave a provisional map. Rice attributed barnacle arrangement to settlement and survival under particular tides and weather.
significance: Hesse, Allee and Schmidt's 1937 textbook Ecological Animal Geography credited the 1935 monograph with applying Petersen's methods to the bottom animals of Puget Sound, while cautioning that further study was required. Barnes and Barnes (1956) relied on the 1925 and 1930 papers for the Puget Sound distribution and conditions of the barnacle *Balanus glandula*. Benson's history of intertidal zonation (the banding of shore life by height) records that by 1928 Shelford had abandoned his physiological study of zonation at the laboratory, saying more natural history of intertidal communities was needed. Benson does not name the 1925 or 1935 papers.
fhl_tie: The survey was done at FHL, then the Puget Sound Biological Station. The 1925 paper covers the area most visited by station classes and investigators and is a joint station and University of Illinois contribution. The 1935 monograph extends the survey across the San Juans in summers 1926–1930, also uses dredging with classes, and thanks director T. C. Frye for support, the boat and equipment. It adds comparisons from Barkley Sound and southern California. Shelford held an Illinois post and spent summers at the station. The biome concept is not a station result: Clements and Shelford's Bio-Ecology dates it to 1916, and Kendeigh's profile puts Shelford's start in community ecology at Chicago.

title: Marine borers and the 1957 symposium
people: Martin W. Johnson, Robert C. Miller, Dixy Lee Ray, Jean R. Julian, Daniel E. Stuntz, Frank H. Johnson
summary: Researchers tracked when wood-boring sea animals settle on Friday Harbor wharf timbers, examined how one of them digests wood, and met at the labs for a 1957 symposium. In 1928–29 Martin Johnson and Robert Miller followed the seasonal settlement of shipworms, barnacles and other wharf-pile organisms. Johnson's 1933–34 test blocks showed most *Limnoria lignorum*, a wood-boring crustacean, settling from January to July, and he advised protective paints at the season's start. In 1952 Dixy Lee Ray and Jean Julian reported cellulase, an enzyme that breaks down cellulose, in the animal's gut, against Yonge's 1927 report of none, cautioning that this did not show it depends on cellulose. Ray organized the international symposium, helped by port, shipyard and wood-preserving money, and edited its 1959 volume. Ray and Daniel Stuntz reported in 1959 that *Limnoria* attacked and lived in sterilized wood without fungi, against other groups' reports, and wrote that this did not close the case.
significance: Reviewing the volume in 1960, P. A. Hartman (Quarterly Review of Biology) judged its cellulase section enough alone to justify publication, and J. W. Hedgpeth (AIBS Bulletin) wrote that almost everyone working on marine borers attended and that marine biologists should have it in their libraries. Ray and Julian's note has 59 citing works in OpenAlex, including a 2020 review by Bredon and colleagues that cites it for *Limnoria* digesting cellulose without microbes. Later evidence for a microbe-free gut and the animal's own enzymes came from others: Boyle and Mitchell in 1978 and King and colleagues in 2010, whose paper does not cite the note.
fhl_tie: Johnson's 1933–34 blocks hung from the Friday Harbor wharf, and he thanks T. G. Thompson for laboratory facilities there. The 1928–29 work with Miller was also at Friday Harbor. The sources do not establish whose wharf either study used. Ray and Stuntz state that their fungi study was done at the labs and the Stazione Zoologica di Napoli. The symposium met at the labs, and the volume's front matter marks its papers as contributions from them, though chapters include outside work such as Becker's in Berlin-Dahlem. Frank Johnson and Ray's 1962 note carries a Friday Harbor Laboratory address. Ray and Julian's 1952 note is addressed from Seattle and does not say where the work was done.

title: Predator-prey experiments on barnacles and *Thais*
people: Joseph H. Connell
summary: Joseph Connell concluded that predatory snails limit where the barnacle *Balanus glandula* can live on San Juan Island. Its larvae settle across the whole intertidal zone, the shore between the tides, yet barnacles reach maturity only in a narrow band at the top of the shore, except where predators are scarce or excluded. Using cages on the shore, he measured the feeding rates of the snails *Thais lamellosa* and *T. emarginata* (*Thais* was later placed in *Nucella*).
