His 1970 paper reported that existing snail populations could account for all of the barnacle deaths low on the shore in mid and late summer, but not for those higher up. He judged that the snails' autumn move up the shore very probably removes the remaining barnacles within a year. He contrasted this with Scotland, where competition for space largely sets barnacle distribution.
significance: In 1971 P. K. Dayton, who had lab space at FHL, called Connell's 1970 paper an intensive study showing that many facets of the distribution of *Balanus glandula* on San Juan Island result from predation by three *Thais* species. Dayton also credited Connell's 1961 and 1970 papers with showing that excluding predators greatly reduces barnacle mortality. Connell mentored Dayton, so this credit is not fully independent. The 1970 paper has 479 citations in the OpenAlex database. Connell's wider reputation rests on his Scottish and Australian work, and his 2020 Nature obituary does not mention San Juan Island or FHL.
fhl_tie: Connell was on the UC Santa Barbara faculty, not FHL staff. Only one source places his work at the station: FHL's centennial timeline by Mills and Hermans lists his predator-prey studies on the wall under the cantilever pier and at Millport, Scotland, in a 1950s entry with no specific year. A 1964 notice of his Mercer Award says he worked on barnacles at Friday Harbor, naming the place and not the laboratories. Two later accounts place him at FHL for a social gathering, dated 1960 in one and 1963 in the other, without mentioning his experiments. The abstract of his 1970 paper names San Juan Island and not FHL. The award itself was for a 1961 paper, and his 1961 papers on competition and predation came from his PhD work at the University of Glasgow and the Millport station, not from FHL.

title: Scuba and the subtidal food webs of the San Juans
people: Paul Sund, Michael Neushul, Karl P. Mauzey, Charles Birkeland, Paul K. Dayton, Norman A. Engstrom, Robin Elahi, Kenneth P. Sebens, Kevin R. Turner, Timothy R. Dwyer, Ross Whippo, Staci McMahon, Sarah Tanja
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: From 1954, divers linked to FHL recorded seaweed communities and who eats whom below low tide around the San Juan Islands and Puget Sound, and some of their records became baselines for measuring change. In 1954 Paul Sund did the first scuba research at the labs, relating invertebrates to the type of sea bottom, and then dived for his master's research on the anemone *Stomphia*. Michael Neushul began scuba work on seaweeds around 1960, and his 1967 paper described seaweed communities from survey lines off Brown Island. Karl Mauzey's 1966 study of the sea star *Pisaster ochraceus* was not a scuba study: he skin-dived at high tide to watch the animals feed on the shore. In a 1968 paper, Mauzey, Charles Birkeland and Paul Dayton used scuba to record the diets of 18 sea star species in Washington state. In 1974 Birkeland estimated growth and predation rates for a sea pen and seven of its predators. A 1982 paper by Birkeland and colleagues followed a sea cucumber and its sea star predators for about 11 years. In 2013 Robin Elahi and colleagues compared 1969–74 photographs of Birkeland's rock-wall plots with surveys from 2008–11 and cautiously inferred that change had been limited.
significance: A 2023 paper by Galloway and colleagues, with one FHL coauthor, counts the 1968 paper by Mauzey, Birkeland and Dayton among the foundational field accounts of sunflower star diet. A 2012 paper by Mah and Blake cites the 1968 paper and Birkeland's 1974 paper for what several sea star families eat. OpenAlex, a citation database, lists 322 citations for the 1968 paper. At the labs the early dives became baselines. The 2013 study by Elahi and colleagues reused Birkeland's photographs, and a 2021 FHL class report by Whippo and colleagues, not peer reviewed, repeated three of Neushul's survey lines. The class report noted the introduced seaweed *Sargassum muticum*. It also described much reduced bull kelp, but only as a qualitative observation; its quantitative comparison did not show the reduction.
fhl_tie: Sund's 1954 dives were the first scuba research at the labs, not the first anywhere: he had learned to dive at UC Santa Barbara in 1952. Three papers came from work done at or from the labs, and each names FHL: Mauzey's 1966 study at Lonesome Cove, the 1982 study by Birkeland and colleagues at Eagle Point, and the 2013 study by Elahi and colleagues at Shady Cove, on the labs' preserve, and at other sites. Neushul left the University of Washington's botany department for UC Santa Barbara in 1962, his Brown Island surveys ran in 1962–63, and the sources do not establish an FHL role in his 1967 paper. The abstracts of the 1968 paper by Mauzey, Birkeland and Dayton and of Birkeland's 1974 paper name Washington or Puget Sound, not FHL. The link of those two papers to FHL rests on the labs' centennial timeline, which lists thesis scuba research at FHL by their authors but names no papers, and on the 1982 paper's use of the 1968 paper's map and San Juan diet data.

title: Sea urchin grazing and algal succession
people: Robert T. Paine, Robert L. Vadas
summary: Keeping sea urchins off rock and out of tide pools changed which seaweeds grew: algal species increased at first, then a few brown algae took over, a replacement sequence known as succession. Robert Paine and Robert Vadas ran the experiments from 1964 to 1967. In the San Juan Islands, divers cleared boulders below the low-tide line and kept urchins off by monthly removal or wire cages. The cages worked poorly, since small urchins passed through the mesh and others ate the plastic coating. Tide pools at Mukkaw Bay supplied the shore half of the study. *Nereocystis* and then *Laminaria* came to dominate underwater and *Hedophyllum* in the pools, while grazed control plots stayed sparse. The 1969 paper concluded that intermittent browsing could add to the variety of coexisting algae. In laboratory tests published in 1977, Vadas found that urchins ranked *Nereocystis* highest and *Agarum* lowest. Preferred algae were absorbed better and gave faster growth and larger gonads.
significance: Sousa, Schroeter and Gaines (1981) modeled their southern California urchin experiments on the 1969 paper and on papers by Dayton (1975) and Paine (1977). Pearse and Hines (1979) cited the 1969 paper for the *Nereocystis*-to-*Laminaria* sequence and noted that Foreman (1977) found a slower sequence in another part of Puget Sound. Bob Steneck, a Paine collaborator, called it classic in a 2016 memorial and said it got scientists thinking about how animals feeding on other organisms affect diversity. That paper was not the first urchin removal: Kitching and Ebling (1961) and Jones and Kain (1967) came earlier. The 1969 paper has about 520 citations in OpenAlex and 330 in Crossref.
fhl_tie: The underwater half of the 1969 paper used FHL. Its plots lay "near the Friday Harbor Laboratories," director R. L. Fernald gave permission to use the labs' facilities, and an NSF grant to the labs helped fund it alongside Paine's own grants. Vadas also coauthored a 1967 physiology paper with an FHL heading, and the labs' own centennial timeline by Mills and Hermans lists his scuba thesis research there. The Mukkaw Bay pools were outer-coast work, and both authors gave UW Seattle addresses in 1969. Sources on the 1977 paper name the San Juan Islands but no laboratory, so the site of those feeding tests is not established. Later FHL kelp studies cite this work, which shows its use at the labs.

title: Disturbance and space on rocky shores
people: Paul K. Dayton, Robert T. Paine, A. J. Kohn, Robert L. Fernald, Joseph H. Connell, Linnea Dayton
summary: Paul Dayton concluded that Washington's rocky-shore community is marked by continuous disturbance and abundant free space shared by many species. For his University of Washington doctoral thesis he worked from 1965 to 1970 at eight shore stations ranked by their exposure to waves. The ranking ran from Tatoosh Island, where he did no experiments, to Colin's Cove. He used cages to keep out limpets and predatory whelks, removed the sea star *Pisaster*, and fired nails into rock to measure strikes by drifting logs. Once they had grown too large for limpets and whelks to threaten, the mussel *Mytilus californianus* and the barnacle *Balanus cariosus* could take all the space, but *Pisaster* and log damage generally prevented this. He also concluded that competition was important in nature mainly where these dominant species escaped those threats, as at Turn Rock, which logs did not strike.
significance: Dayton's 1971 paper in Ecological Monographs won the Ecological Society of America's Mercer Award, which Wikipedia dates to 1974. Bruce Menge, a fellow graduate student, says he designed his 1976 study in New England to be like Dayton's. The society's centennial list of notable papers, chosen mostly by citations, includes the paper. It has 1,570 citations in Crossref and 2,393 in OpenAlex, two citation databases. Credit for the shift toward field experiments is shared. Peter Raimondi, a former student of Joseph Connell, places Dayton with Connell and with Dayton's advisor Robert Paine in that shift, and Dayton says that he and his peers did not create such experiments.
fhl_tie: Three of Dayton's eight stations were in the San Juan Islands: Eagle Point and Turn Rock, at both of which he removed *Pisaster*, and Colin's Cove, about 200 m north of FHL's Cantilever Pier. FHL director Robert Fernald provided laboratory space and facilities at FHL. Of the four National Science Foundation research grants Dayton acknowledged, one was a training grant to FHL. Joseph Connell, who designed the cages, helped Dayton make cage parts in the Friday Harbor shop. The tie is partial. Dayton says he chose Washington in order to work at Friday Harbor, but he was enrolled on the main campus in Seattle and taught there, and his 1971 paper gives his address as the Department of Zoology at the University of Washington in Seattle. The other five stations were on the Olympic Peninsula, including Mukkaw Bay, the site of Robert Paine's 1966 *Pisaster* experiments, which were not FHL work.

title: Kelp carbon and otter-urchin-kelp food webs
people: David O. Duggins, Charles A. Simenstad, James A. Estes, James E. Eckman, Amy T. Sewell, Megan N. Dethier, Kevin H. Britton-Simmons, Aaron W. E. Galloway
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: David Duggins and colleagues tested how sea otters, by eating urchins that graze kelp, control Alaskan kelp forests, and traced kelp carbon into coastal animals. In work published in 1980, Duggins removed urchins at Torch Bay, Alaska, predicted what returning otters would do to kelp, and checked these predictions where otters had been transplanted. In the Aleutians in 1985–87, Duggins, Charles Simenstad and James Estes used islands with and without otters as a natural experiment. Caged mussels and barnacles grew two to five times faster at kelp-dominated islands, and carbon isotopes, markers of diet, placed kelp carbon throughout the food web. Estes and Duggins's 1995 monograph tested the otter-urchin-kelp pattern at 153 Alaskan sites. In the San Juan Islands, Duggins and James Eckman measured how understory kelps, low kelps near the bottom, alter water flow and the growth of animals below them, and how currents and grazers affect kelp survival. Later papers from FHL tracked detached drift seaweed down to 170 m with a remotely operated vehicle and showed that fatty acids can tell seaweed groups apart.
significance: Krumhansl and Scheibling's 2012 review credits Duggins and colleagues' 1989 Science paper with linking high production in Alaskan mussels and barnacles to a food subsidy from nearby kelps. That paper itself presents its data as support for earlier suggestions by K. H. Mann. A 2004 paper led by Estes, Duggins's coauthor, bases its account of the otter-urchin-kelp pattern on a 1974 paper by Estes and Palmisano and on the 1995 monograph. The report's census counts 696 citations for the 1989 Science paper and 798 for the monograph. Which food source matters most is debated and differs by place. A 2016 FHL Tide Bite article, written by a member of the FHL lab Duggins co-led, reports that Lowe and colleagues in 2014 found phytoplankton the most important source of essential fatty acids for filter feeders in the San Juan Islands.
fhl_tie: The Alaskan fieldwork was not done at FHL. Torch Bay was surveyed in the late 1970s, around Duggins's 1979 start as an FHL marine technician while a graduate student. The tie to FHL is his FHL address from 1981 onward, including on the 1989 Science paper and the 1995 monograph. FHL's bibliography lists his 1980 and 1983 papers, but whether they carry an FHL address is not established. Duggins's coauthors Simenstad, Estes and Eckman were based elsewhere, and Estes led the monograph. The understory, flow and drift-seaweed work came from FHL. Its 1991, 2001 and 2003 papers and the 2012 fatty-acid paper name study sites in the San Juan Islands. The exact sites of the 2012 remotely operated vehicle survey, in a basin in Washington State, and of the 2016 paper on experimental seaweed islands are not established.

title: Inducible defenses and changeable form in colonial animals and seaweeds
people: C. Drew Harvell, Stephen R. Palumbi, Kathryn L. Van Alstyne, Colin W. Clark, Dianna K. Padilla, Erika V. Iyengar
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Colonial animals and seaweeds can change form in response to predators, damage or waves. In 1984 C. Drew Harvell reported laboratory experiments in which attack by nudibranchs (sea slugs) rapidly induced defensive spines in the bryozoan *Membranipora membranacea*, a colonial animal. Her abstract says such defenses were previously known only in plants and two groups of tiny animals. That year Stephen Palumbi reported moving genetically identical sponge fragments between rough and calm water, and they stiffened quickly. His 1986 paper traced the stiffening to the number and size of the sponge's skeletal needles. Harvell's 1986 paper found that spines cut nudibranch feeding to about 40 percent of normal, but spined colonies initially grew at 85 percent of the unspined rate. In 1989 Kathryn Van Alstyne reported that damage induced branches in the seaweed *Fucus distichus*, and snails preferred these branches less than normal tips. Harvell's 1992 paper found smaller growth differences in the field than short-term laboratory tests predicted, and her model with Colin Clark that year set out when an induced defense works better than a constant one.
significance: Harvell's 1990 review drew sustained citation, with 513 citations counted by Crossref and about 1,700 by OpenAlex. Independent authors cite the original papers as examples of induced form: Brown, Wilson and Gagnon (2019) and Rennolds and Bely (2023) cite Harvell's work on spines, and DeBiasse and Hellberg (2015) cite Palumbi's work on sponges. Credit for first reporting such spines is shared with Yoshioka. Harvell's 1981 thesis cites Yoshioka's 1973 UC San Diego dissertation on nudibranch-induced spines in *Membranipora serrilamella*. A 2002 paper by Iyengar and Harvell records that Yoshioka, in a 1982 paper, noticed that spines in *M. membranacea* correlated with a nudibranch. How far Harvell's 1984 paper went beyond Yoshioka's 1982 paper is not established.
fhl_tie: Harvell's 1984 paper and Palumbi's 1984 and 1986 papers list FHL and University of Washington zoology addresses, and Harvell later called her nudibranch and bryozoan work "my PhD research at FHL." The sources name no site for her 1984 experiments or Palumbi's transplants, so where they ran is not established. Harvell's 1986 paper and her two 1992 papers are linked to FHL only by their listing in the station's bibliography, and her 1990 review has a Cornell address. The work for her 1981 University of Alberta master's thesis on another bryozoan was done largely under FHL's breakwater and the Friday Harbor town docks. Later *Membranipora* papers include Harvell and Padilla's 1990 paper, which reports censuses on Turn Island, Harvell's 1998 paper on a population at FHL, and Iyengar and Harvell's 2002 paper on experiments run at FHL in 1996–1997. The first two of these have Cornell addresses. Van Alstyne's 1989 paper reports experiments at FHL and a survey on Tatoosh Island.

title: Functional groups of seaweeds
people: Robert S. Steneck, Megan N. Dethier, David O. Duggins, Sally D. Hacker, M. M. Littler, D. S. Littler, L. Watling, Dianna K. Padilla, Bengt J. Allen, J. C. Phillips, G. A. Kendrick, P. S. Lavery
summary: In 1994 Robert Steneck of the University of Maine and Megan Dethier of FHL argued that a few shared traits, more than species identity, set the structure of seaweed communities. Their idea extended models from the early 1980s, by M. M. and D. S. Littler and by Steneck with L. Watling, based on form or on functional groups, meaning sets of species that share traits. Dethier's related Washington experiments include removing chitons (grazing mollusks) and kelp in the San Juan Islands with David Duggins (1985) and transplanting crust-forming seaweeds, which showed wide variation within that one group (1994). Steneck and Dethier's joint 1994 paper sorted seaweeds into groups from microscopic algae and filaments to crusts, with a typical productivity, lifespan and canopy height for each. Its graphical model uses two factors, potential productivity and disturbance by grazers, to predict which groups a community will contain. Drawing on Maine, Washington and the Caribbean, the authors reported patterns more stable and predictable for groups than for species, without claiming to have tested the model.
significance: Steneck and Dethier's 1994 paper has about 1,150 citations in OpenAlex and 925 in Web of Science. Cappelatti, Mauffrey and Griffin (2019) cite it first when calling the sorting of species into coarse functional groups the usual approach in seaweed ecology. The model was also contested. Padilla and Allen (2000), writing from Stony Brook, argued that the model does not adequately describe how abundant the groups are in any of its three regions. Phillips, Kendrick and Lavery (1997) found in Western Australia that 14 of 82 species did not clearly fit any group and that working at the group level lost information. They also said that testing the general model was not their intention.
fhl_tie: FHL's part is partial. Megan Dethier, one of the 1994 paper's two authors, was based at FHL, with FHL addresses on her papers from 1981 and an FHL postdoctoral fellowship in 1983. Robert Steneck, the paper's contact author, was at the University of Maine. Web of Science lists FHL for the paper along with a University of Washington institute and a University of Maine center, without matching addresses to authors. The paper is a three-region synthesis rather than fieldwork at the station, and the Washington shores behind its data are not established. The earlier models it extended are not among FHL's recorded publications. Two related San Juan Islands papers (1985 and 1991) carry FHL addresses. Dethier's 1984 tidepool paper gives an FHL address, but its subject matches her 1981 University of Washington dissertation, and its abstract places the pools only on the coast of Washington.

title: What deposit feeders select and digest
people: Robert F. L. (Liko) Self, Peter A. Jumars, Lawrence M. Mayer, Linda L. Schick, Stephen Sampson, Zhen Chen
summary: Most deposit feeders tested, animals that eat sediment, selected particles by size, and gut fluids released food and metals. In 1988 Liko Self and Peter Jumars of the University of Washington offered 11 species beads with no food value. Eight selected the beads by size, with a peak near 6 micrometers, a result the authors called a modest advance. Lawrence Mayer's group in Maine, with Jumars and Self, then tested which food in sediment a gut can reach. In 1995 they reported that a protein-cutting enzyme released amino acids at rates similar to gut juice of the sea cucumber *Parastichopus californicus*, the only animal compared, and said the method may not mimic all deposit feeders. In 1996 they reported that gut fluids dissolved orders of magnitude more copper and lead than seawater was predicted to dissolve, but typically only about 1–10 percent of the total contaminant load. A 1997 survey of 19 species found the strongest gut surfactants (detergent-like compounds) in deposit feeders. In 2004 Jumars's lab reported a limit on the 1988 peak, which came from smooth beads: on natural silts and sands, one worm species peaked at 80–99 micrometers.
significance: The 1995 and 1997 papers, which thank FHL, have 192 and 168 citations in the report's census. Dauwe and colleagues (1999), at the Netherlands Institute of Ecology, credited papers by Mayer and colleagues from 1986 and 1995 with the enzyme method and applied it to five North Sea sediments; they thank Mayer for comments on a draft. A 2003 National Research Council report named extraction with digestive fluids, one tool among many, as explaining how available at least some metals are to organisms. It cited Mayer's 1996 paper and a 1999 paper by Zhen Chen and Mayer, neither established as FHL work, and said simple correlations between amounts extracted and amounts animals accumulate are rare.
fhl_tie: The authors worked from Seattle and Maine, with no FHL address shown; FHL provided facilities for part of the work. Jumars's own account says a 1978 study of Skagit flats animals showed the need for more species, and that need began the lab's seasonal moves to FHL. The 1995 paper from Lawrence Mayer's group built its test mainly on Maine sediment, calibrated it with gut juice from *Parastichopus* collected near San Juan Island and mailed frozen to Maine, and thanks director A. O. Willows for use of FHL. The group's 1997 paper thanks FHL's Director; 12 of its species came from Puget Sound and 7 from Maine, with no finer site given.
