title: Marine invaders: jellyfish, sea squirts and a San Juan seaweed
people: Kevin H. Britton-Simmons, Gretchen Lambert, Charles C. Lambert, Claudia E. Mills, Freya Sommer, Lauren Stefaniak, Stephan Bullard
summary: In a 1995 paper, Claudia Mills and Freya Sommer reported two jellyfish species, believed native to the Black Sea, found in San Francisco Bay tributaries in 1992 and 1993. That paper contained errors, which Mills and John Rees corrected in 2000. Charles and Gretchen Lambert surveyed southern California harbors from 1994 to 2000 and showed that nonindigenous (introduced) sea squirts made up a major part of the mass of organisms growing on floating docks. Mills also helped start the 1998 Puget Sound Expedition, which found 40 nonindigenous species. From 1999 Kevin Britton-Simmons removed the introduced seaweed *Sargassum muticum* from plots at two San Juan sites. Competition from the seaweed cut native canopy algae (the taller seaweeds) by about 75 percent, apparently through shading, and indirectly reduced sea urchins. Gretchen Lambert compared the body structure and type specimens (the reference specimens for species names) of a colonial sea squirt reported under different names worldwide, some of them her own misidentifications. With DNA work led by Lauren Stefaniak, she concluded in 2009 that it is one species, *Didemnum vexillum*, probably native to Japan.
significance: An independent 2015 review of sea squirt invasions by Zhan and colleagues follows Gretchen Lambert's 2009 paper and the 2009 paper by Stefaniak and colleagues on the name *Didemnum vexillum*. It cites the Lamberts' 2003 paper for California's nonindigenous sea squirts. Two independent 2006 papers cite Britton-Simmons's 2004 paper: Scheibling and Gagnon name it among the exceptions in a field where rigorous experimental testing lagged behind observation, and Strong and colleagues list it among the few ecological studies of the *Sargassum muticum* invasion. A 2007 review by Purcell and colleagues cites the 1995 Mills and Sommer paper for both San Francisco Bay species in its table of jellyfish introductions.
fhl_tie: Kevin Britton-Simmons's research was based at FHL and used its boats, dive facilities and lab space, but his 2004 paper gives the University of Chicago as his address, with FHL as his present address. The 1998 Puget Sound Expedition, sponsored mainly by a Washington state agency, worked up its samples at FHL, and FHL-based Claudia Mills was among its originators. The other ties are weaker. The jellyfish in the Mills and Sommer paper were collected in California. The Lamberts met as FHL summer students in 1964, and FHL sources call Gretchen Lambert both a longtime visitor and a long-time researcher. The Lamberts ran all but the summer 2000 California survey from Cal State Fullerton on outside funds. In the jellyfish and sea squirt papers, FHL's documented part is FHL addresses and space at its Whiteley Center for preparing Gretchen Lambert's 2009 paper. The DNA work, in a separate 2009 paper, was led from the University of Connecticut.

title: Marine biomechanics
people: M. A. R. (Mimi) Koehl, Stephen A. Wainwright, Steven Vogel, Michael LaBarbera, Catherine Loudon, R. S. Alberte, Jon D. Witman, Thomas H. Suchanek, Emily Carrington, Kenneth P. Sebens, Michael J. O'Donnell, Matthew N. George, Sam Van Wassenbergh, Adam P. Summers
summary: Work linked to FHL measured how sea anemones, kelp and mussels bear water forces and how pipefish strike. In her 1976 Duke thesis and 1977 papers, Mimi Koehl treated anemones as cantilevers, beams fixed at one end, comparing a tall species from calm water with a short species from surge channels. With Stephen Wainwright she found that stems of the bull kelp *Nereocystis luetkeana* stretch 38 percent on average before breaking. Wainwright, Steven Vogel and Koehl taught the first FHL biomechanics course in 1979. In a later offering of the course, Jon Witman found that kelp on mussels from the lab dock raised the flow forces on the mussels two- to sixfold. In 1988, Koehl and R. S. Alberte showed that flat kelp blades bundle together, which cuts drag but shades them more, while ruffled blades stay spread out and flap. In 2008, Sam Van Wassenbergh and colleagues linked the fast strike of the bay pipefish, *Syngnathus leptorhynchus*, to elastic recoil of tendons, which snap back like springs. In 2013, Michael O'Donnell, Matthew George and Emily Carrington showed that the threads mussels anchor themselves with are weaker when made under high carbon dioxide levels.
significance: In his 2007 history, Steven Vogel recalls that Koehl's thesis examination prompted the Duke course that became comparative biomechanics. He dates the field's effective founding to James Gray at Cambridge in the 1930s, traces the later surge to Duke, and does not mention FHL. FHL's milestones page says the field arose from graduate training and research at FHL, and its newsletter counts course alumni among the field's who's-who. In 2020, Coleman and Martone built their kelp research on Koehl and Alberte's 1988 paper. In a 2011 review, Roberts and Azizi cite the 2008 paper's figure for the pipefish, a peak of more than 5,000 watts per kilogram of muscle modeled from one fish, when describing fish that appear to feed using elastic power amplification, the fast release of energy stored in springy tissue.
fhl_tie: Most sources date the first FHL course to 1979; two FHL documents give 1974 and 1980. Witman's flow tests, most of Vogel and Catherine Loudon's study of a red alga and the 2013 mussel-thread study were done at FHL, and several chapters of Vogel's 2003 book Comparative Biomechanics were written there. Work on mussel attachment in Witman's paper also used Tatoosh Island. Koehl's anemone papers give Duke as her address and FHL, where she was a postdoctoral fellow, as her present address. Two of them thank FHL for facilities, and the work also used Tatoosh, a University of British Columbia lab and Duke. Her kelp paper with Wainwright came out of Duke, but it used FHL facilities and kelp surveys made in 1975 near FHL and on Tatoosh. The 1988 paper with Alberte gives Berkeley and Chicago addresses. Later papers by Koehl place that paper's flow and blade measurements near FHL and in San Juan Channel, but the sources do not establish where its drag and photosynthesis tests were done. The 2008 pipefish paper gives no FHL address and names no filming site. Two of the fish studied came from Friday Harbor and others from Elkhorn Slough, and the paper thanks FHL staff and students for help in summer 2006.

title: Flow near the seabed, recruitment and the racetrack flume
people: James E. Eckman, Peter A. Jumars, Arthur R. M. Nowell, Robert F. L. (Liko) Self, María Cristina Gambi, David O. Duggins, Amy T. Sewell, Christopher E. Siddon, Terrie Klinger
summary: This work measured how flow just above the seabed affects where sediment and young bottom animals settle, and it gave FHL a large flow tank, or flume. From the late 1970s Peter Jumars and Arthur Nowell's lab in Seattle brought flow tanks to FHL. In 1980 James Eckman began experiments on a Skagit Bay sandflat, planting straws that mimicked bulrush and measuring their effect on flow in a flume. His 1983 paper treated flow as the baseline explanation to test. Sediment and several groups of organisms matched predictions for passive dispersal by the water, while some patterns of recruitment, the arrival of young animals, did not. A 1984 National Science Foundation grant helped fund a new laboratory at FHL, Lab 7, to house a large racetrack flume. In that flume María Cristina Gambi measured flow through eelgrass. She separated a high-shear zone at the top of the canopy, where speed changes sharply with height, from a low-shear zone below it. In papers from 1989 onward David Duggins and Eckman asked how low-growing kelps in the San Juan Archipelago alter flow, the settling of particles, recruitment and growth, and later how currents and grazers affect kelp survival.
significance: Butman's 1987 review of larval settlement named Eckman's 1983 paper, along with studies by Baggerman (1953), Eckman (1979) and Hogue and Miller (1981), as field support for the passive accumulation of larvae. The review credited Eckman's flume experiments for the specific predictions he made in advance. The report's census counts 453 citations for Eckman's 1983 paper. Peterson and colleagues (2004) reanalyzed Gambi's flume results to test their model of flow reduction in seagrass canopies, and the census counts 430 citations for Gambi's 1990 paper. That paper followed seagrass flow work by Fonseca and colleagues in 1982, which a 2019 paper co-written by Fonseca credits with showing high shear moving from the sediment surface to the canopy top.
fhl_tie: The parts of this work placed at FHL are Lab 7, its racetrack flume and the eelgrass measurements, which Gambi's 1990 paper states were made in that flume. The paper's authors, Gambi, Nowell and Jumars, gave addresses in Ischia and Seattle; Nowell and Jumars were based in Seattle. Liko Self, the technician and coordinator of their lab, supervised its trips to FHL, which are known from participants' own account. Eckman's field work was in Skagit Bay. His 1983 paper gives a Seattle address and thanks FHL for laboratory facilities, but it does not say where his smaller flume stood. The kelp work ran in the San Juan Archipelago. Its 1989 and 1990 papers list David Duggins and Amy Sewell at FHL and Eckman at Skidaway Institute of Oceanography. Skidaway held a grant for the kelp work, and current meters for a 2003 paper were calibrated there. The 2001 kelp paper does not say where its racetrack flume was, and Skidaway also had one.

title: How medusae swim and feed: rowing versus jetting
people: John H. Costello, Sean P. Colin, M. D. Ford, John O. Dabiri, Kakani Katija, Kelly R. Sutherland, Brad J. Gemmell, Kevin T. Du Clos, Claudia E. Mills
summary: A series of studies sorts medusae (jellyfish) into two swimming types: bullet-shaped (prolate) species jet and disc-shaped (oblate) species row, and the difference broadly tracks how they feed. Jet propulsion long served as the model for how medusae swim. In 1981 Claudia Mills, working at FHL, named swimming pattern as one of seven factors in feeding efficiency. Ford and Costello (2000) found that prolate medusae contract along the whole bell and make a narrower, faster jet, while oblate medusae contract near the margin and make a broader, slower one. Colin and Costello (2002) showed in six species that jet thrust explains acceleration only in prolate medusae. The wakes of oblate medusae carried swirls of water at the bell margin, consistent with rowing. Costello and Colin (2002) found that the six species' diets split along the same line: ambush-feeding jetters took mainly crustaceans and single-celled ciliates, and cruising rowers took mainly soft-bodied prey. *Proboscidactyla*, intermediate between the two forms, was among the ambushers. Dabiri and colleagues (2010) linked the type of wake to foraging in seven species, with one exception. Katija and colleagues (2011) measured the flows around the medusa *Aequorea victoria* to map the water it encounters. Studies from 2015 to 2022 extended this analysis to siphonophores, colonies that swim with many jets.
significance: Meech's 2022 review in the Journal of Experimental Biology says jet propulsion was long thought to be the principal thrust mechanism in jellyfish, and it credits Colin and Costello (2002) with showing that jet propulsion alone cannot model flatter medusae. Pallasdies and colleagues (2019, eLife), modelers outside this group of authors, cite the same paper for the distinction between rowing and jetting. Sørnes and colleagues (2008) cite it among studies linking hunting style to bell shape but say the scheme needs refinement: the jellyfish *Periphylla* is prolate and so expected to ambush, yet it swims constantly. The report's census gives 172 citations for Colin and Costello (2002) and 122 for Dabiri and colleagues (2010).
fhl_tie: Apart from Claudia Mills, the authors give addresses away from FHL. Their animals came mostly from FHL's docks or the waters at Friday Harbor, and some studies were also done at least partly at FHL. Mills made her 1981 observations at FHL, and her paper lists both the University of Victoria and FHL. Katija and colleagues (2011) made flow measurements at FHL and prey-capture measurements at Woods Hole. The 2015 and 2019 siphonophore studies took colonies from FHL docks and thank FHL for facilities, and the 2022 study filmed colonies collected at FHL. The core jetting and rowing papers establish where the animals came from, not where they were filmed. Colin and Costello (2002) collected at an FHL dock in 1992–94 and Dabiri and colleagues (2010) in 2007, and neither paper thanks FHL. Ford and Costello (2000) name only Friday Harbor waters. Costello and Colin's 2002 diet paper places its collecting beside FHL's docks.

title: Northern clingfish suction
people: Dylan K. Wainwright, Thomas Kleinteich, Anja Kleinteich, Stanislav N. Gorb, Adam P. Summers, Petra Ditsche
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Northern clingfish (*Gobiesox maeandricus*) hold on with a suction disc to rough surfaces where manufactured suction cups fail, and that grip inspired cups that attach to rough surfaces. Dylan Wainwright and colleagues (2013) pulled euthanized fish off eight clean resin casts of differing roughness in a materials tester. The fish held on all eight at 80–230 times body weight, weakest on the smoothest, while manufactured cups in seawater held only on the three smoothest. Petra Ditsche and colleagues (2014) added surfaces fouled for six weeks in the sea. Holding force fell on rough fouled surfaces but stayed near 150 times body weight. Ditsche and Adam Summers (2019) removed part of the disc's margin, showing it is critical on rough surfaces. They then built two-material silicone cups, the best holding 60–70 kilopascals (a unit of pressure) on surfaces up to about 270-micrometer grain, the roughest tested.
significance: Sandoval and colleagues at UC San Diego (2019), who cite the 2013 and 2014 papers, designed their own clingfish-inspired disc. A 2023 review of fish adhesion by Wang and colleagues describes the 2019 cup among such devices. Arnette and colleagues (2025), with support from an FHL endowment, call the species a common model for bio-inspired suction cups. The 2013 and 2014 papers have 176 and 109 citations in the report's census. A University of Washington video about the 2014 paper won a prize in the 2016 Ocean 180 science communication video contest.
fhl_tie: The 2013 result grew from Wainwright's summer 2011 FHL student project, with fish caught at Dead Man's Cove or beside the FHL dock. All 2013 authors but Gorb and all 2014 authors list FHL, some alongside Duke, Harvard or Kiel, and a journal news note places the surface fouling at FHL. The 2019 paper lists FHL first for both authors, Alaska Anchorage second for Ditsche, and held its fish in FHL tanks. Earlier, a 1967 study by Arita in British Columbia had tested dead fish and proposed suction. The sources do not establish where the materials tester stood, where the 2013 viscosity tests and electron microscopy were done, or where the cups were built, though UW News says Ditsche started the work as an FHL postdoc.

title: Photoelectric measurement of light in the sea
people: Victor E. Shelford, Floyd W. Gail, Jakob Kunz, Marvin Williams, Clinton L. Utterback
summary: Photoelectric cells, devices that turn light into an electric current, were lowered from boats around Friday Harbor in 1920 to measure how much daylight enters the sea and how that relates to where seaweeds grow. In 1918 Floyd Gail had concluded from experiments based at the Friday Harbor station that light is a controlling factor in the lower limit of the brown seaweed *Fucus*, the greatest depth at which it grows. In summer 1920 Gail and Victor Shelford worked from a steamboat and a towed scow with cells built by Jakob Kunz. Their 1922 paper reported that the sea surface shut out about 25 percent of midday light in calm weather and 60 to 70 percent or more in rough water, and it related the zones of brown and red algae to the measured light. Readings reached 120 m, though the authors considered those below 25 m too few for certainty. Shelford and Marvin Williams each published a paper on light in Puget Sound waters in 1929. Clinton Utterback studied variation in solar light at the station in 1932, and a timeline of the station's history lists his 1935 summer course as Penetration of Light.
significance: A 1931 paper by Gall and Atkins credits Shelford and Gail with the first use of photoelectric cells to measure light under water, while Shelford and Gail's own 1922 paper reports an earlier electrical attempt, Regnard's 1889 selenium cell at Monaco. In 1926 Poole and Atkins found that surface losses were in most cases smaller than those in the 1922 paper, and they said the unshielded cell used in that work made those figures harder to interpret, though they noted that the 1922 work reached much greater depths than their own measurements at Plymouth. Gall and Atkins trace the apparatus built for the research ship Atlantis to Poole's 1925 design, used near Plymouth. The Atlantis apparatus copied the Plymouth one and was not modeled on the Friday Harbor rig.
fhl_tie: Shelford and Gail's 1920 readings were made around Friday Harbor in a summer when both were listed to teach at the station there. Their joint 1922 paper acknowledges work done at Friday Harbor, and its tables carry the place names Point Caution and Brown Island. Gail's separate 1922 paper places the study at the station, though it dates the study to June and July, while the joint paper dates the readings July 18 to August 3. The site of the deepest readings is not stated. Calibration and much of the calculation were done at the University of Illinois. Gail worked at the station in summer 1918, with field sites on San Juan, Brown and Sucia islands and at Turn Rock. Utterback's 1932 study was made at the station. The 1929 papers by Shelford and Williams ran in the station's publication series, but the sources do not establish where those measurements were made.

title: The San Juan Channel seawater and plankton series
people: Martin W. Johnson, Thomas G. Thompson, Seldon P. Todd, Lyman D. Phifer, H. H. Gran, E. C. Angst
summary: Scientists at the Friday Harbor station, called the Puget Sound Biological Station until 1930, built two multi-year records of San Juan Channel's seawater and studied its plankton. Martin Johnson's plankton samples there date to 1924 and 1926–1929. From September 1926, Thomas Thompson, Johnson and Seldon Todd measured temperature, chlorinity (a measure of salt) and density at the station and in the channel, with weekly plankton tows. Reports ran to September 1929, adding pH, oxygen, phosphate and silicate for part of that period. Johnson's 1932 plankton account described an unidentified egg, which he assigned in 1934 to the small crustacean *Tortanus discaudatus*. H. H. Gran of Oslo coauthored papers on diatoms (single-celled algae) and taught his version of Lohmann's centrifuge method, which Lyman Phifer used. Phifer and Thompson analyzed a second run, 1931–1935, sampled every four or five days from late 1931. They reported surface oxygen seldom above 80 percent saturation and nutrients never low enough to limit phytoplankton.
significance: The Oceans (Sverdrup, Johnson and Fleming 1942), a book Johnson coauthored, selected Friday Harbor as an example of the annual cycles of nitrate, phosphate and silicate, plotting monthly means from the 1931–35 series beside English Channel data. Authors whose publications show no tie to the station also used it as a reference record: Allee and colleagues (1949) for seasonal nitrate, Black and Dewar (1949) on seaweed chemistry, and Ketchum, Vaccaro and Corwin (1958) on the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus.
fhl_tie: Sampling was done at the station: in 1926–27, hourly there and daily and weekly in the channel off its float. Johnson's plankton hauls and first egg hatchings were at Friday Harbor. Phifer and Thompson's series used a pier at the laboratories. Both authors had Friday Harbor bylines and Phifer was resident assistant director, though the paper does not name who took the samples. The first report, in 1928, has a University of Washington byline. Gran visited from Oslo; accounts differ on the years, and his centrifuge teaching is known from Miller's in-house account (1940). Johnson's 1934 paper has a Seattle byline, thanks director Thompson for laboratory facilities and does not say where the 1933 egg work was done.

title: Thompson's seawater chemistry
people: Thomas G. Thompson, Bertram D. Thomas, Clinton L. Utterback, Rex J. Robinson, Phoebe Blalock, Seldon P. Todd, George H. Hitchings
summary: Thomas G. Thompson, a University of Washington analytical chemist, developed better ways to measure trace elements in seawater, among them iron, manganese, boron, silicon and copper. In 1926 and 1927 his group sampled Argyle Lagoon. A 1927 paper by Thompson and two coauthors reported a steady sulfate-to-chloride ratio of 0.1396 in North Pacific and Puget Sound waters, close to Dittmar's earlier figure, which when recalculated came to 0.1394. George Hitchings's first papers rest on work he did at the station in summer 1927; the research recognized by his Nobel Prize came later, at the Wellcome Research Laboratories, where he worked from 1942. In 1934 Thompson, Bertram Thomas and Clinton Utterback tabulated how the electrical conductivity of seawater varies with chlorinity and temperature. The group's records of the water off the station are in the entry on the San Juan Channel series.
significance: A 1973 National Academy of Sciences memoir, two of whose three authors were Thompson's doctoral students, calls the trace-element work his most important contribution to the data of science and says the conductivity study supplied basic data for modern salinity methods. The 1942 book The Oceans, two of whose authors had FHL ties, cites these papers alongside parallel work by Moberg, Rakestraw and others. Thompson received the Agassiz Medal in 1948 and joined the Academy in 1951. Independent support for the conductivity claim is narrower: a 1971 review by Tucker pointed users to the 1934 tables where top accuracy was not needed, a 1972 paper by Gopinathan and Qasim reports later corrections to those tables, and Millero's 2010 history credits 1950s instruments for precise salinity measurements.
fhl_tie: Samples from the San Juan Archipelago in summer 1926 went into the 1927 sulfate paper. Thompson's group sampled Argyle Lagoon and the channel off the station from 1926 and published in the station's series from 1927. Thompson directed the Oceanographic Laboratories, which included the station, from 1930 or 1931 (sources differ) to 1951. The National Academy memoir treats Seattle as the institution and Friday Harbor as a summer field station, and the sources do not place the trace-element methods or the conductivity measurements at the station. One 1931 wire report says work at Friday Harbor prompted a $250,000 Rockefeller gift, $200,000 of it for a Seattle building; the Foundation's own report names the station but does not give its work as the reason.

title: Jellyfish blooms and gelatinous predators
people: Claudia E. Mills, David Wrobel, Richard D. Brodeur, Robert H. Condon
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Claudia Mills studied how jellyfish and similar animals feed and asked if their numbers are rising worldwide. In 1981, from observations on a dock at FHL and in a tank, she proposed that swimming behavior, beyond tentacle number and length, shapes how four hydromedusae (small jellyfish) feed. Her 1995 paper, using submersible cruises and gut contents, argued, against earlier work by Parsons and Greve, that gelatinous predators matter in productive and unproductive seas. In 1998 she and David Wrobel published a guide to 160 Pacific Coast species, and she began a web list of valid ctenophore (comb jelly) names that she reports other databases draw on. A 1999 paper by Richard Brodeur, Mills and others reported a rise in Bering Sea jellyfish, and a 2012 synthesis notes a later decline. Her 2001 review sorted reports into native increases, climate-linked fluctuations, introductions and declines, and stressed how few data exist. Her 2009 web page reports large declines in 30 years of Friday Harbor data on the jellyfish *Aequorea* and describes the data as not fully analyzed. Her publication list includes no publication of these data.
significance: The 2012 synthesis, by a working group of the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS), with Mills as a coauthor, concluded that belief in a global rise in jellyfish is unsubstantiated. Among the origins of the idea, it named a 1993 paper by Parsons, then Mills's 1995 paper together with a 1998 paper by Pauly and colleagues. It cited her 2001 review, with other work, for proposed causes and reported declines. That review has 562 citations in the report's census and 480 in Crossref. The question stayed contested: a 2013 analysis by Robert Condon and coauthors, without Mills, found no robust global increase, while a 2012 study by Brotz and coauthors reported increases in 28 of 45 large marine ecosystems.
fhl_tie: By her own account, Mills has been resident at FHL since 1978, apart from visiting stints. FHL's share of the work has four parts. She made the 1981 dock observations as a University of Victoria PhD student on Canadian funding. Her salinity experiments published in 1984 used animals collected near FHL and in Mitchell Bay. The 1995 paper includes her 1987 Friday Harbor diet data. Photographs for the guide were taken in an FHL cold room, though how many is not established. Her 1995 and 2001 papers give FHL as her address but rest largely on cruises off New England, in the Alboran Sea and in the Gulf of Maine, and on reports from around the world. The Bering Sea data in the 1999 paper came from NOAA trawl surveys. The 2012 synthesis came from the NCEAS group, and the 2013 analysis thanks Mills but does not name FHL.

title: Polymer gels in seawater
years: 1998 (Seattle); FHL program from 2001–2002; papers giving an FHL address 2003–2022
people: Pedro Verdugo, Yong-Xue Ding, Anthony G. Rodriguez, Iván Quesada, Wei-Chun Chin, Mónica V. Orellana, John I. Hedges, Alice Alldredge, Farooq Azam, David Kirchman, Uta Passow, Peter Santschi
summary: Organic polymers dissolved in seawater can self-assemble into tiny gels, a possible bridge between dissolved and particulate carbon. Dissolved organic matter is a large carbon pool that lasts longer than particles do. Aggregation of colloids (very fine particles) was thought to help turn it into particles, but assembly from free polymers had not been shown. In 1998 Wei-Chun Chin, Mónica Orellana and Pedro Verdugo, working in Seattle, showed that free polymers do assemble spontaneously into gels, using filtered water from Puget Sound, the North Pacific and the Arctic. Verdugo then moved his program to Friday Harbor. A 2004 review estimated about 70 billion metric tons of gel carbon, if about 10 percent of surface dissolved organic matter formed gels across the whole ocean. Verdugo's lab went on to make preliminary tests of colonization by bacteria (2006), develop a test that measures gel carbon (2007), and show that a polymer released by the bacterium *Sagittula stellata* induces assembly (2008). Later estimates of gel carbon differ: Verdugo's 2012 review gives about 10 billion tons and his 2021 paper about 70 billion.
significance: The work applied polymer physics to the exchange between dissolved and particulate organic matter. The 2004 review has 691 citations, 17th among the 25 most-cited papers in the report's census. A review by Decho and Gutierrez (2017) cites the 1998 paper and Verdugo's work and calls gel formation a process of significant importance. How large the effect is remains open. Verdugo said in 1998 that a carbon-removal role was not proved. Orellana, a coauthor of the 1998 paper, and Hansell wrote in 2021 that the contribution of gels to dissolved carbon processes is essentially unknown. Quigg et al. (2021), with Chin and Santschi among the authors, say particles identified by staining have not been shown to have the gel properties the 1998 paper defined.
fhl_tie: The central 1998 finding was not made at FHL. The Nature paper gives only a Seattle address and predates Verdugo's FHL program: his NSF award is dated 2001, and the FHL timeline lists his move under 2002. The paper also credits others, including Alldredge, Passow and Logan, with the idea that colloids and larger particles could be viewed as gels. FHL's part lies in the work that followed, and only some of that is placed at the station. The 2008 study's acknowledgments place it in Verdugo's FHL lab, as part of a Florida State PhD under Chin. A 2010 review's acknowledgments say the work it covers was done largely at FHL with Chin's lab. Undergraduate apprenticeships on gels ran at FHL in 2003–2006, and the colonization tests used San Juan Channel water and FHL dock bacteria. A 2003 paper on ultraviolet light and the 2007 gel-carbon test paper are tied to FHL by author address only. Only Verdugo among the 2004 review's authors gave an FHL address, and the review acknowledges a symposium partly financed by FHL.

title: Bull kelp studies and carbon monoxide in the float
people: T. C. Frye, George B. Rigg, Annie L. Fallis, Sarah M. Sheldon, Sanford M. Zeller, Abigail Neikirk, Lola B. Brown, Annie May Hurd, Joanne Karrer, Seth C. Langdon, W. R. Gailey, Grace E. Howard, Harry Andrews, Leona Sundquist, Emmett T. Bodenberg, Lena A. Hartge, Lyle A. Swain
summary: Investigators at the Friday Harbor station used bull kelp (*Nereocystis luetkeana*) as an experimental plant and reported carbon monoxide in its gas-filled float. Their work from 1914 to 1938 produced about 20 papers, most of them in the station's own series. Annie Fallis and Sarah Sheldon measured the growth of the blade and the stalk. T. C. Frye measured the gas pressure in 1,000 floats from a rowboat, and Annie May Hurd tested the effects of light, tension, depth and fresh water. In 1916 Seth Langdon rechecked gas analyses by Sanford Zeller and Abigail Neikirk and found 1 to 12 percent carbon monoxide in nearly 1,000 plants. He backed the finding with blood tests and by killing a guinea pig, a canary and a chick in the gas. In 1918 Langdon and W. R. Gailey replaced the gas in the floats of cut plants tethered in the sea. They attributed the carbon monoxide to respiration, as George Rigg had suggested. Harry Andrews later counted the animals living in the holdfasts, the structures that anchor the kelp, and Lena Hartge cultured the kelp's small sexual stage.
significance: A 1975 technical report by Whyte and Englar credits the station with many early biological studies of the kelp and with the carbon monoxide finding. A 2020 paper by Liggan and Martone says that Langdon's 1917 paper first noted the high levels of carbon monoxide, and it traces to him the saying among algae specialists that a float holds enough of the gas to kill a chicken. The explanation of where the gas comes from was not settled. In 1976 Foreman proposed that it is a by-product of autolysis, a cell's self-digestion, linked to respiration, although Langdon and Gailey had found no carbon monoxide from ground kelp undergoing autolysis. Liggan and Martone measured about 1.2 percent carbon monoxide and 60 percent oxygen, and they suspected that earlier samples had been contaminated with air.
fhl_tie: Several authors say their work was done at the station: Sheldon in 1914, Frye in 1915, Hurd in 1916 and 1918, Langdon and Gailey in 1918, Rigg in 1919, Emmett Bodenberg in 1927, and Rigg and Lyle Swain in 1937 and 1938. Fallis's paper also places her experiments at Friday Harbor. Grace Howard and Leona Sundquist only began their work there. Rigg's 1917 paper used a Seattle kelp bed, and Hartge's cultures began in Seattle and continued at the station in 1927. Papers by Zeller and Neikirk, Lola Brown, Joanne Karrer and Andrews do not name the station as their site. The site of the work in Langdon's 1916 and 1917 papers is not established, although Rigg and Swain in 1941 and Whyte and Englar in 1975 place his work at the station. Liggan and Martone's measurements used kelp from British Columbia.

title: Kylin's red algae of Friday Harbor
people: Harald Kylin
summary: Harald Kylin's 1925 monograph cataloged the red algae of Puget Sound and described 31 species and three genera, largely from material he collected on two summer visits to Friday Harbor. Kylin, a Swedish specialist in algae and a professor at Lund, spent ten days at the Puget Sound Biological Station in July 1922. He returned from June 14 to July 28, 1924, the first summer on the station's permanent campus, to teach marine algae, and took his preserved collection to Sweden. The monograph lists 128 red algae for Puget Sound, leaving out the chalky coralline algae: 103 from his own specimens, 57 of them already known there, and 25 from the literature or other collections. Ten of the 31 species had been reported under incorrect names. The genera are *Thuretellopsis*, *Opuntiella* and *Pugetia*.
significance: G. F. Papenfuss, in the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, lists the monograph among Kylin's contributions to regional knowledge and places his greatest work in the form and classification of a large group of red algae. It has 56 citations in the report's census, 1944 to 2024, a few apparently counted in error. Later work revisits its species: Carlile and colleagues (2010), using reference (type) specimens, found *Ceramium washingtoniense* and *C. pacificum* to be one species, and Ahmed and colleagues (2024), with an FHL coauthor, sequenced *Rhodochorton tenue* from the FHL preserve and supported treating it as distinct from *R. purpureum*.
fhl_tie: Kylin collected at and around the station as a visitor, in 1922 on a US tour that also took in Monterey, La Jolla and Woods Hole, and in 1924 while teaching. Thirty of his 31 species rest on that collection, and the other on Whidbey Island material he did not collect. He examined the algae and signed the monograph in Lund, also using earlier records, including Muenscher's in the station's publications. His 1923 monograph on red algal development was already in press during the 1922 trip. Papenfuss says material from his stops fed monographs through 1932, but not how much came from Friday Harbor. The station's timeline gives the 1922 stay as several weeks; Kylin's preface says ten days.

title: Shore classification, monitoring methods and armoring
people: Megan N. Dethier, Linda Kunze, Elizabeth S. Graham, Sarah Cohen, Lucinda M. Tear, Rebecca J. Allee, Steven N. Murray, Richard F. Ambrose, Wendel W. Raymond, Jason D. Toft, Jeffery R. Cordell, Andrea S. Ogston, Sarah M. Heerhartz, Aundrea N. McBride, Helen D. Berry, Hugh Shipman
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Megan Dethier devised a way to classify the marine and estuarine shores of Washington State, then with colleagues tested how shores are surveyed and measured what seawalls and other armoring do to beaches. Her 1990 state report sorted about 60 habitats by depth, bottom material and other features, adding wave and current energy to the Cowardin wetland scheme. A 1993 study compared judging percent cover (the share of a plot a species covers) by eye with counting random points. On computer-drawn plots of known cover, visual estimates were more accurate and repeatable. On a rocky shore they were more repeatable for rare species and about twice as fast. She co-wrote a proposed national classification (2000), a federal methods report (2001) and the handbook Monitoring Rocky Shores (2006). Paired surveys of armored and unarmored Puget Sound beaches (2016) found fewer logs, less wrack (stranded seaweed) and fewer high-shore invertebrates, with larger effects where armor sat lower on the beach.
significance: The Encyclopedia of Puget Sound derives shore classes from the 1990 system; its maps combine that system with Washington's ShoreZone shoreline data and match neither exactly. UW's Puget Sound Institute commissioned Dethier's 2014 update. The Salish Sea Wiki calls the 1990 report "a seminal work." The 1993 paper has 488 citations in the report's census and reached rangeland science in a 2021 study by De Stefano and colleagues, but its result is unsettled. A 1992 comparison by Meese and Tomich had favored digitized photos, De Stefano and colleagues call point methods generally more objective and precise, and Murray's chapter in the 2001 federal report calls visual estimates generally less accurate, Dethier's paper excepted, and disputes the time saving.
fhl_tie: Dethier was based at FHL and wrote there. A later reprint of the 1990 report gives her FHL address and credits FHL facilities for most of the writing, though its core scheme came from talks with state agency staff. The 1993 paper thanks FHL for space but had federal funding, National Park Service site access and coauthors at Princeton, Stanford and UW Seattle. The 2000 proposal lists her at FHL but came from a national workshop. The 2001 report thanks FHL for support during her two chapters; Murray and Ambrose wrote the others. Where the handbook was written is not established. She led the armoring work at FHL, but surveys ran across Puget Sound and the only other FHL coauthor was Raymond.

title: Ocean acidification experiments
people: Michael J. O'Donnell, Matthew N. George, Emily Carrington, James W. Murray, Emily A. Roberts, Terrie Klinger, Kenneth P. Sebens, Kit Yu Karen Chan, Daniel Grünbaum, Emma Timmins-Schiffman, Carolyn S. Friedman, Steven B. Roberts
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Mussels from San Juan Island, tested at FHL, made weaker anchoring threads in more acidic seawater. Work from summer 2009 by Kit Yu Karen Chan, Daniel Grünbaum and Michael O'Donnell found that sand dollar larvae under high carbon dioxide (CO2) were narrower and had smaller stomachs, but their swimming speed did not change significantly. FHL received a National Science Foundation award in 2009 and in 2011 finished a shared laboratory with CO2-controlled aquaria, in-water enclosures and a chemistry lab. Emma Timmins-Schiffman and colleagues found that oyster larvae studied in July 2011 developed late under high CO2. In a 2013 paper, O'Donnell, Matthew George and Emily Carrington let mussels regrow their attachment threads for 20 days at nine pH levels (a lower pH is more acidic). Threads made at high CO2 more often failed at the adhesive pad, and modeled attachment strength fell about 40 percent, with no change in growth. Seawater measurements from 2011 to 2013 at the FHL dock, led by James Murray, averaged pH 7.8, an acidity owed mostly to natural respiration in the waters that supply the area.
significance: The 2013 mussel paper tested a material that is not calcified, when by its own account most acidification studies focused on calcium carbonate, the mineral of shells. In a 2013 press account in The Tyee, University of British Columbia ecologist Chris Harley praised that step and the wide range of pH levels. A 2015 review by Haigh and colleagues cites the 2013 mussel paper for thread weakening, and the report's census counts 165 citations of that paper. Later studies differ. A 2017 study by Zhao and colleagues found weaker attachment in the mussel *Mytilus coruscus*, while a 2018 study by Clements and colleagues found no CO2 effect in the mussel *Mytilus edulis* at 16 and 22 °C and noted that the 2013 work ran at 10 °C.
fhl_tie: The mussel experiment and the dock measurements were done at FHL. The methods section of the 2013 mussel paper names FHL only for holding the animals, and all three authors give FHL addresses. A 2015 account by Laura Newcomb of Carrington's group places the pH trials in FHL's acidification laboratory. James Murray of the University of Washington (UW) led the dock measurements with coauthors affiliated with FHL. The two larval papers have a less direct link: each thanks FHL for laboratory space and includes O'Donnell, then at FHL, as a coauthor. The sand dollar work predates FHL's acidification laboratory, and its water chemistry was analyzed at NOAA. The oyster work was led from UW's fisheries school, and where each step was done is not established. O'Donnell's earlier papers on sea urchins and on a culture system (equipment for rearing animals) came from UC Santa Barbara groups and are not FHL work.

title: Sea star wasting and marine disease ecology
people: Morgan Eisenlord, Maya Groner, C. Drew Harvell, Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria, Ann Jarrell, Jason Hodin, Carolyn Friedman, Steven Roberts, Colleen Burge, Melanie Prentice, Alyssa-Lois Gehman
summary: Researchers working partly at FHL tracked a sea star wasting outbreak, raised some of the animals used to test a bacterial cause, and linked a wasting disease of eelgrass, a seagrass, to warmer water. Groner and colleagues surveyed San Juan Islands meadows in 2012, within FHL's summer disease course, taught from 2010, and an NSF research network, and their 2014 paper tied the disease to larger, older leaves. Eisenlord and colleagues followed ochre stars in Washington through the 2014 outbreak and reported in 2016 that the risk of disease rose with body size and temperature. Adult stars in the San Juan Islands fell to one quarter of their earlier numbers, though numbers on the outer coast did not decline. A 2021 paper by Groner and colleagues linked warmer water in the prior month to more common eelgrass disease, and warming to lower severity. Hodin's team at FHL reported progress in 2021 toward raising sunflower stars through a full captive life cycle. In a paper published in 2025, Prentice and colleagues reported that injecting sunflower stars with a cultured bacterium, *Vibrio pectenicida* strain FHCF-3, reproduced the wasting disease.
significance: The 2025 paper by Prentice and colleagues moved the search for a cause from a densovirus, a type of virus, to a bacterium that can be grown in culture. The paper says later evidence refuted the densovirus. Rebecca Vega Thurber of UC Santa Barbara, who was not involved in the work, told a KUOW reporter that it was much more convincing than the earlier densovirus study. The finding is contested. In 2026, Work and colleagues argued that compelling evidence would require a case definition, meaning agreed criteria for what counts as the disease, that incorporates microscopy. Prentice and colleagues agree that a definition would be useful, but reply that its absence does not refute the finding in sunflower stars.
fhl_tie: FHL hosted the temperature tank experiment in the 2016 ochre star paper, whose lead authors were at Cornell and the University of Prince Edward Island. For the 2014 eelgrass paper, shoots were held at FHL and the tissue work was done at Cornell. For the 2021 eelgrass paper, leaves were measured at FHL, but no author gave FHL as an address. FHL gave logistical support to a meeting of the NSF network where a 2016 review of marine disease emergencies was conceived; Cornell held the network's grant. Hodin's program at FHL supplied test stars in 2023 and 2024 and two diseased stars sampled for the bacterial cultures. The 2025 paper by Prentice and colleagues was led from the University of British Columbia, where samples were processed, and the Hakai Institute, with experiments at U.S. Geological Survey facilities at Marrowstone. Coauthors Drew Harvell and Hodin write in a newsletter that the FH in the strain name FHCF-3 stands for Friday Harbor; the Prentice paper does not explain the name.

title: Rearing the sunflower star
people: Jason Hodin, Alexi Pearson-Lund, Fleur Anteau, Pema Kitaeff, Shannon Cefalu, Richard Strathmann, Sherry Tamone, Donald Greer
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: An FHL team led by Jason Hodin set out to rear the endangered sunflower star (*Pycnopodia helianthoides*) in captivity through its whole life cycle, from egg to egg. The team collected adult stars around San Juan Island from March 2019. The earliest fertilization listed in the team's 2021 paper, on July 26, 2019, used gonads (reproductive organs) mailed from Alaska. Fertilization with San Juan Island parents followed on November 5. Injecting adults with a hormone to trigger spawning rarely worked in those early attempts, so the reared cultures came from gonads in amputated arms, which the adults began to regrow. A 2025 paper by Hodin and colleagues reports that injection has since worked consistently in the January–April peak spawning season. The 2021 paper reports rearing juveniles to one year after they settled on the bottom. Twenty captive-bred stars were released off the FHL dock in 2024, and the news accounts cited here give no survival figures for them. Twenty more were released off Decatur Island in April 2026. Divers found 14 of those 20 by May, with no signs of disease.
significance: The 2021 paper from Hodin's team reports culturing juveniles of this species for the first time. Donald Greer had reared it through metamorphosis (larva to juvenile) in 1962, from adults kept at FHL. FHL's 2024 newsletter claims the first rearing through the full life cycle, but the 2021 paper states that as a goal, and no paper cited here documents it. A 2025 Mongabay article instead describes a California coalition as breeding the species "for the first time." A 2024 Orange County Register article credits FHL's 2019 work as the start of an aquarium program called SAFE. A 2025 study by Prentice and colleagues tested a bacterial cause of sea star wasting disease partly on FHL's captive-bred stars, and coauthor Drew Harvell named access to the right test animals as a reason for the team's success.
fhl_tie: San Juan Island adults were held at FHL, and the breeding program, the released stars and the 2021–2023 warming experiments on larvae and juveniles (the Star Power study) were based there. The Nature Conservancy was the main funder, and the Samish Indian Nation provided the boat, captain and lead diver for the 2026 release. Some of the work took place elsewhere. The Alaskan gonads were shipped from Juneau, the first juvenile cultures were kept at a site without flowing seawater before moving to FHL, and permits let the operation move between Friday Harbor and Seattle. The 2025 Prentice study, told in the entry on marine disease, was led from elsewhere.

title: The June 2021 heatwave on Salish Sea shores
people: Wendel W. Raymond, Megan N. Dethier, Julie S. Barber, Hilary A. Hayford, Christopher D. G. Harley, Teri L. King, Blair Paul, Camille A. Speck, Elizabeth D. Tobin, Ann E. T. Raymond, P. Sean McDonald
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Record air temperatures in late June 2021 coincided with the year's lowest tides, and a rapid survey recorded how shellfish in and around the Salish Sea, the inland waters of Washington and British Columbia, fared. Wendel Raymond and ten coauthors sent the survey to a regional network from central British Columbia to Willapa Bay. Local scientists rated shellfish condition on a five-point scale against what they knew as normal for each site and species, giving 203 observations from 108 sites and 24 species. Condition tended to be worse on inland shores, where the air was hotter and low tide fell near solar noon, about four hours later than on the outer coast. Bay mussels fared worse than California mussels, and high-shore barnacles worse than lower-shore clams and oysters. The authors call the ratings coarse, and the ratings are not mortality counts. A 2024 analysis of clam and oyster surveys, which covered less than a quarter of the original survey's north-south range, found highly variable effects.
significance: The Fifth National Climate Assessment (2023) cites the survey's 2022 paper in its accounts of shellfish die-offs in the 2021 heatwave (Chapters 2 and 15). The paper has 128 citations in the report's census, most from outside the author group. Later work by some of the same authors qualified that paper's findings. The 2024 analysis, by Raymond and coauthors, did not find statistical support for the broad negative effects on clams and oysters described in the 2022 paper, a result it attributed to variable survey data and possibly its own limited scope. A 2025 study by a team that included Raymond and Megan Dethier found Salish Sea sites hit harder than the Olympic coast, with most shore communities largely recovered by summer 2022.
fhl_tie: Wendel Raymond, an FHL research scientist, analyzed the data and wrote the 2022 paper. Raymond and coauthor Megan Dethier both list an FHL address on that paper, and its contributions statement credits all eleven authors with conceiving the work. The observations came from more than 28 people in 19 organizations across the region, with Washington Sea Grant funding. The paper's main text describes no fieldwork or facilities at the station, so FHL's part, as far as that text shows, is the role of these two authors. Raymond's address on the 2024 follow-up paper lists the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife first and FHL second, and Raymond's address on the 2025 follow-up lists that department alone.

title: The station's Publications and early regional monographs
people: T. C. Frye, Ida Shepard Oldroyd, T. S. Oldroyd, Mildred Bush, Belle A. Stevens, C. H. O'Donoghue, Elsie O'Donoghue, Annie May Hurd, Edwin Chapin Starks
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: The Friday Harbor station published its own series from 1915 to 1931, seven volumes of research papers and regional reference works. T. C. Frye, the station's director from 1914 to 1930, edited the series, first called Puget Sound Marine Station Publications and later Publications Puget Sound Biological Station. The report's census lists 149 items from the series. Fifteen of these have titles about bull kelp (*Nereocystis luetkeana*), and Annie May Hurd's 1916 paper is one example. The reference works included Mildred Bush's identification key to the echinoderms, the group of sea stars and sea urchins, published in 1918 and revised in 1921. They also included Ida Oldroyd's Marine Shells of Puget Sound and Vicinity (1924), which covers about 520 mollusk species in 272 pages. Belle Stevens's paper on hermit crabs and C. H. and Elsie O'Donoghue's list of bryozoans, small colonial animals, followed in 1925. Earlier, and outside the series, Edwin Starks collected fishes around the San Juan Islands in 1909. His survey, published in 1911, listed the fishes known from Puget Sound and described three rockfish species.
significance: Independent evidence comes from later use. A 1975 report by Whyte and Englar says many early bull kelp studies were done at the station. Other works cite kelp papers from the series: a Lenfest Ocean Program synthesis on bull kelp cites those by Brown and by Hurd, and a 2026 paper by Breitkreutz and Martone cites Frye's 1930 paper on kelp blades. The citation index OpenAlex lists 12 works citing Oldroyd's monograph and 6 citing Starks's survey. The World Register of Marine Species accepts as valid Stevens's hermit crab genus *Orthopagurus* and Starks's rockfish *Sebastes emphaeus*. The warmest praise is not independent: the University of Washington's 1925 yearbook said the series made the station "better known in foreign countries" than the university, and FHL's own milestones page calls it an early definitive chronicle of regional research.
fhl_tie: The series was the station's own, but its editor, Frye, the station's director, worked at the University of Washington in Seattle, and it also carried work from elsewhere, such as a list of lichens from southeast Alaska. Contributors' ties to the station varied. Stevens collected around Friday Harbor in the summers of 1922 and 1923. Bush, of the University of Washington, used material from San Juan County, and her 1921 revision names the station in its byline. The Oldroyds, of Stanford, spent several weeks at Friday Harbor and at Canada's Nanaimo station in June and July from 1917 to 1920. The O'Donoghues, of the University of Manitoba, spent a few hours at Friday Harbor in 1921 and two years later dredged in Griffin Bay and off Point Caution, working from the Nanaimo station. Starks collected in 1909 as a member of the station and used its dredging steamer, in a summer when the station had partly moved to Olga. Outside funds paid for his netting, and University of Kansas zoologists supplied one rockfish specimen.

title: Comparative embryology and the Northern Pacific Coast manual
people: W. J. Baumgartner, Robert L. Fernald, Arthur H. Whiteley, Richard A. Cloney, Fu-Shiang Chia, Megumi F. Strathmann
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: The labs taught embryology, the study of how animals develop from eggs, in summer courses across more than a century, and Megumi Strathmann's 670-page book of 1987 collected data and methods on the eggs, embryos and larvae of Northern Pacific Coast marine invertebrates. The course appears by 1910, when W. J. Baumgartner taught it, and the report's class table lists it in 59 years through 2019. Robert Fernald, director from 1960 to 1972, taught it with Arthur Whiteley in 1960 and encouraged faculty to bring in co-teachers from around the world. Richard Cloney taught the course 17 times by the FHL timeline's count, though the class table names him in only 6 years, and used electron microscopy to study cell movements in the metamorphosis of ascidians (sea squirts). Fu-Shiang Chia came as a graduate student in 1959 and returned to teach it. The book opens with a chapter of general procedures, then 31 chapters by animal group, some by other authors, including Cloney on ascidians.
significance: FHL's centennial timeline by Mills and Hermans credits Fernald and his graduate students with developing the discipline at the labs "to a level of distinction." That is the station's own view: FHL people, helped by the Strathmanns and Whiteley, compiled the timeline, and Mills wrote a chapter of the book. Outside credit rests on the book: 962 citations in OpenAlex under its 2017 reprint. Collin et al. (2021, International Journal of Developmental Biology) cite it on how long larval development lasts, without discussing FHL.
fhl_tie: The courses were taught at the station. The centennial timeline places Strathmann and Fernald in Lab 6 in 1982 putting the book together, and says it incorporated FHL embryological lore and laboratory techniques, with chapters by FHL scientists. A library catalog entry credits text contributions and advice from Fernald's colleagues and students. Cloney's metamorphosis work is only partly tied to FHL. He held a University of Washington zoology post in Seattle, and of the ten species tested with the drug cytochalasin B in a 1973 paper, three came from near the labs and seven from Woods Hole. That paper's author addresses include Seattle, Woods Hole and Friday Harbor.

title: Kozloff's keys and guides to Northwest marine life
people: Eugene N. Kozloff, Linda H. Price (later Beidleman), C. E. Mills, R. L. Miller, C. P. Staude
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Eugene Kozloff turned identification keys, step-by-step guides for naming a specimen, into printed manuals for the marine invertebrates of the Pacific Northwest. His guide for general readers, Seashore Life, appeared in 1973 and in expanded form in 1983. Keys to the Marine Invertebrates of Puget Sound appeared in 1974. With Linda Price and taxonomic specialists he revised and expanded it as Marine Invertebrates of the Pacific Northwest (1987), reissued in 1996 with 30 pages of additions and corrections. The publisher says it covers close to 4,000 species of the shore and shallow water from southern Oregon to the Queen Charlotte Islands. Separately, on July 14, 1962 Kozloff found orthonectids, tiny parasites of marine invertebrates, in bristle worms dredged near Dot Rock in the San Juan Archipelago. By his account the group was known only from European waters and one report near Woods Hole. He named the new genus *Ciliocincta* in 1965 and in 1992 distinguished four genera in the group.
significance: Dave Cowles's Invertebrates of the Salish Sea, a site sponsored by Walla Walla University's Rosario Beach Marine Laboratory, calls the 1987 manual the primary reference for keying Pacific Northwest invertebrates, and its page for the sea star *Pisaster ochraceus* uses the manual as its key. OpenAlex gives the manual 194 citations in the report's census, 61 of them from 2012 through 2025, though that count may combine the 1987 and 1996 printings. The World Register of Marine Species lists *Ciliocincta* as an accepted genus.
fhl_tie: Kozloff taught summers at FHL in 1961 and 1962 and was resident from 1966 to 2007. FHL's centennial timeline, by insiders Mills and Hermans, says the 1974 and 1987 books incorporated keys held in draft at FHL for decades. The publisher says zoologists associated with FHL and several other institutions developed them over more than 30 years, so the books centered on FHL without being exclusive to it. FHL's bibliography lists sections of the 1987 manual by C. E. Mills, R. L. Miller and C. P. Staude. Kozloff names FHL as the place of his 1962 orthonectid discovery. His later orthonectid papers, in FHL's bibliography through 1997, also treat European species and were not all FHL material.

title: Scanning all fishes, oVert and SlicerMorph
people: Adam P. Summers, Sara M. Rolfe, A. Murat Maga, Douglas M. Boyer, David C. Blackburn, Luke Tornabene, Sharlene Santana, Katherine Maslenikov
tie: based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
tie_label: Based at FHL, work partly elsewhere
summary: Work at FHL produced a free online collection of 3D X-ray scans of fishes and contributed to a wider scanning project and to open software to measure them. This is a method and an open dataset rather than a discovery. In 2015 a micro-CT scanner, which builds 3D images from X-rays, was installed at FHL as the centerpiece of the Karel F. Liem imaging facility. Adam Summers used it to speed up a batch method begun on hospital scanners, rolling many fishes into one scan, and posted results as #ScanAllFish, aiming at every fish species. The sources do not report that goal as met. From 2017 to 2023 the facility was one of six scanning centers for openVertebrate (oVert), a National Science Foundation (NSF) project led from the Florida Museum. University of Washington (UW) News credits the FHL team with more than 7,200 of oVert's 13,000-plus specimens. SlicerMorph, an open add-on to the 3D Slicer software for retrieving and measuring scans, was funded from 2018 and described in a 2021 paper.
significance: Blackburn and colleagues (2024), in a review of oVert coauthored by Summers, report more than 200 peer-reviewed publications citing data from all oVert sites together. Groups outside FHL credit #ScanAllFish directly. Schnetz and colleagues (2019) took CT scans of six kinds of fish from its archive, and Evans and colleagues (2021) thank oVert and #ScanAllFish for free scanning. A 2020 step-by-step guide to CT data by Buser and colleagues has Summers as its only FHL author. The report's census records 222 citations for the SlicerMorph paper and at least 47 publications naming the Liem facility from 2016 to 2026. These numbers measure use of the method and do not point to any single finding.
fhl_tie: Summers raised money for the scanner and started #ScanAllFish at FHL, where visiting teams also scanned. An FHL team did UW's share of oVert scanning, under an award placed at Friday Harbor. Sara Rolfe, who led SlicerMorph's software, lists an FHL post from August 2018, and the project's website lists meetings there in 2023 and 2025. Elsewhere, Summers's batch scanning began on hospital machines, and DigiMorph, an online CT archive at the University of Texas, was running by 2001. oVert, led by David Blackburn, spanned 18 institutions. A. Murat Maga conceived SlicerMorph in Seattle, with NSF awards to him, Summers and Douglas Boyer at Duke. The oVert review gives no specimen counts by site, so it does not confirm the UW News figure.
